Physicists Discover a Strange Newly introduced Form of Magnetism in a Simple Metal

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Electronics can use more than electrical charge, and evidence of unusual magnetism in europium silicide could help researchers explore how to put electron spin to work.
  • At very low temperatures, a simple metal made from europium and silicon develops a spiral pattern of magnetism that leaves it with no overall magnetization.
  • According to recent reports, an international team has found compelling evidence for this state, called p-wave magnetism, in europium silicide, or EuSi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electronics can use more than electrical charge, and evidence of unusual magnetism in europium silicide could help researchers explore how to put electron spin to work.

At very low temperatures, a simple metal made from europium and silicon develops a spiral pattern of magnetism that leaves it with no overall magnetization. Its electrons nevertheless appear to favor opposite spin orientations when they travel in opposite directions, an unusual relationship that could offer researchers new ways to explore and control electronic behavior.

According to recent reports, an international team has found compelling evidence for this state, called p-wave magnetism, in europium silicide, or EuSi. The findings, published in Nature, provide an experimental foothold in a field where suitable materials have been difficult to find.

In a recent development, spin is a quantum property that gives electrons a magnetic character, somewhat like tiny compass needles. In a conventional ferromagnet, spins tend to align in the same direction, producing net magnetization. In EuSi, between approximately 33 and 62 kelvin, or about −400 to −348 °F, the magnetic moments of europium atoms instead form an ordered spiral. The individual moments are substantial, but their contributions cancel overall.

Recent findings suggest that the predicted relationship between opposite directions of electron motion and opposite spin polarizations is known as an odd-parity spin texture. Finding a material in which researchers can investigate it has been challenging. Previous candidates include electrical insulators and metals that develop magnetic order only at very low temperatures or have additional symmetry complications. EuSi combines a fixed chemical composition with a spiral magnetic phase that has the required symmetry, and researchers can grow high-quality single crystals for experiments.

In a recent development, dr. Erjian Cheng grew those crystals approximately three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden. Initial photoemission experiments, which use light to eject electrons and examine their properties, showed that magnetism had an unusually large influence on EuSi’s electronic band structure, the pattern of energies electrons can occupy inside the material. That raised the possibility that its magnetic order might link spin to the direction of electron motion.

The investigation brought together 38 researchers from 19 institutions, including ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

Combining theoretical calculations with several experimental techniques, the researchers examined both the atomic magnetic arrangement and its effects on electrons. Neutron diffraction revealed the spiral of europium magnetic moments and confirmed that its symmetry met the conditions for p-wave magnetism. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which maps electron energies and momenta, showed that magnetism substantially reshaped the electronic structure, producing energy separations exceeding 100 millielectronvolts.

Sources indicate that measurements that also resolved electron spin supplied a more specific test. The spin polarization changed sign across successive magnetic Brillouin zones, repeating regions in a map of electron momentum defined by the magnetic order. It also weakened sharply near regions where the predicted p-wave spin texture should vanish. Together, these observations provided spectroscopic evidence consistent with the theoretical state.

According to recent reports, “When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons,” explains Cheng. “That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism.”.

The proposed spin pattern arises predominantly from magnetic exchange interactions, which influence how spins arrange themselves, and from the symmetry of the magnetic spiral. That distinguishes it from familiar spin-splitting effects driven mainly by spin-orbit coupling, an interaction between an electron’s spin and its motion.

The spiral also introduces handedness, or chirality. EuSi’s underlying crystal structure is centrosymmetric, meaning that it looks the same when inverted through its center. Its magnetic spiral, however, can twist in either of two opposite senses. Using magnetic force microscopy and spatially resolved photoemission spectroscopy, the researchers identified magnetic domains approximately ten micrometers across.

When examined with circularly polarized light, domains with opposite magnetic handedness showed distinct electronic responses. The results demonstrated that the spiral’s handedness is coupled to the electronic structure, connecting the organization of the atomic magnetic moments with the behavior of the electrons.

“What makes EuSi particularly exciting is that an unconventional electronic spin structure emerges from the magnetic order of a chemically simple metal,” states Prof. Claudia Felser, Director at MPI CPfS. “This demonstrates how the discovery of newly introduced materials can reveal entirely new electronic phenomena. EuSi now gives us an experimental platform to investigate how magnetic symmetry and chirality can be used to control electronic properties, with potential implications for future spintronics and unconventional superconductivity.”.

In a recent development, spintronics uses electron spin as well as electrical charge in electronic devices. The findings could inform that field, along with research on topological quantum materials and unconventional superconductivity. They also illustrate how a solid’s properties depend on its magnetic order and electronic quantum states, alongside its chemical composition and crystal structure.

Reference: “Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi” by Erjian Cheng, Yixing Yang, Yifan Gao, Jan Priessnitz, Yiqing Hao, Jieyi Liu, Rui Lou, Alexander Fedorov, Mengyu Yao, Yuri Prots, Houke Chen, Ralf Koban, Xuemin Shi, Ying-Ting Chan, Ulrich Burkhardt, Berit H. Goodge, Walter Schnelle, Vicky Hasse, Jaafar Ansari, Zhuocheng Lu, Peter Bencok, Gerrit van der Laan, Makoto Hashimoto, Donghui Lu, Jacek Osiecki, Zhanfeng Liu, Shengtao Cui, Jaime Sánchez-Barriga, Oliver Rader, Yulin Chen, Hua Wang, Jiadong Zang, Leila Noohinejad, Weida Wu, Libor Šmejkal, Junwei Liu, Zhongkai Liu and Claudia Felser, 18 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11295-9.

The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

📅 28 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.
  • Sources indicate that the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine.
  • Sources indicate that this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

Sources indicate that the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

Sources indicate that this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We upgrade this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Upcoming to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he introduced Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

According to recent reports, adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he debuted Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

In a recent development, eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

Sources indicate that this diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

Industry observers note that ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the fresh template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

These days, London has no shortage of excellent new-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

It has been revealed that this elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

Industry observers note that since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

It has been revealed that this quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

The area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The newly introduced online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

According to recent reports, chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

According to recent reports, at the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

In a recent development, there is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent Latest York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

After a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

It has been revealed that clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

It has been revealed that while the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most vital British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

It has been revealed that joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand fresh, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

Shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

In a recent development, bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

For my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy new surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

According to recent reports, gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

It has been revealed that chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Recent findings suggest that together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a significant group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

Industry observers note that A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

According to recent reports, this vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips notes Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in fresh-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Sources indicate that must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Recent findings suggest that despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Tech Report: Slingshot Earth: NASA's Europa Clipper Will Gain Speed and Tests Its Instruments During Its Earth Flyby

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Europa Clipper will soon bid farewell to Earth.
  • Gravity maneuvers can be used to either accelerate or decelerate spacecraft, depending on their desired trajectories.
  • The relative velocity is illustrative and does not represent Europa Clipper's velocity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Europa Clipper will soon bid farewell to Earth. On December 3rd, it will conduct its propellant-saving gravity assist maneuver and head for Jupiter. These types of maneuvers are a common part of missions beyond Mars.

Gravity maneuvers can be used to either accelerate or decelerate spacecraft, depending on their desired trajectories. When a mission requires acceleration to the outer Solar System, a spacecraft passes behind a planet's orbital path, and the planet's gravity pulls on it and accelerates it relative to the Sun. The maneuver also changes its trajectory. These maneuvers are the norm for missions beyond Mars.

The relative velocity is illustrative and does not represent Europa Clipper's velocity. Credit: Made with AI.

Industry observers note that âWeâre coming down into the gravity well of Earth, following its curve, and shooting out again,â said Robert Pappalardo, Europa Clipperâs project scientist at NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory. âThe spacecraft is able to get pulled by the gravity of the planet and continue on its way â now with a slightly changed trajectory and moving faster than it was before.â.

It has been revealed that when a mission needs to decelerate into the inner Solar System, the spacecraft passes in front of a planet's orbital path, and the planet's gravity decelerates it relative to the Sun. Bepi-Colombo, for example, relied on multiple gravity-braking maneuvers to slow down enough to orbit Mercury. The Europa Clipper performed one of these earlier in its mission, to set it up for the gravity-assist with Earth.

Sources indicate that the relative velocity is illustrative and does not represent Europa Clipper's velocity. Credit: Made with AI.

The Europa Clipper is NASA's largest deep space mission, and this Earth flyby is critical to accelerating it toward Jupiter. So was its gravity braking maneuver at Mars in March, 2025, which slowed it down so it could perform this upcoming flyby of Earth.

The Clipper's closest approach to Earth will be within 3,140 to 3,450 kilometers on December 3rd, above West Africa, at at 3:14 p.m. EST. In Africa and southern Europe, it should be visible in backyard telescopes.

Even though about half of the Clipper's launch mass is propellant, it needs these flybys to complete its mission. The flybys get it to Jupiter, and the spacecraft is conserving its propellant for orbital insertion at Jupiter, the single largest burn of its mission. Jupiter's gravity well is powerful, and even with all of this propellant to place it in orbit, the Clipper will still perform a gravity breaking maneuver at Ganymede hours before insertion to save a little more propellant. It will enter its Jupiter orbit in April 2030.

Recent findings suggest that the flyby of Earth serves another purpose, too: instrument calibration. All 11 of the Europa Clipper's science instruments will be active during the flyby. The mission has nine science teams organized around the 11 instruments, and each team will take the relevant data and compare it to known data about Earth. That will let them calibrate their instruments to a very fine degree.

âWeâre practicing the intricacies of the operation, but weâre also practicing how to work together to produce the best science,â noted JPLâs Erin Leonard, Europa Clipper project staff scientist. âThe things we practice now will set us up for success at Europa.â.

Since Earth's magnetosphere is so well-understood, this is an especially important opportunity for Clipper to calibrate one of its most important instruments, the Europa Clipper Magnetometer. The central goal of Clipper's mission is to determine if Europa truly does have an ocean under its icy shell, and the magnetometer will be able to do that after multiple flybys. It can also determine the ocean's depth, and even its salinity. It can also help measure the thickness of the icy shell.

In a recent development, this illustration shows what Europa's ocean could be like. Scientist know it has an icy shell, and they know it has a rock core and mantle. There are enticing hints that it has a subsurface ocean, but they aren't sure. Europa will find out. Image Credit: NASA/(Europa Lander Study 2016 Report).

Industry observers note that europa sits inside Jupiter's vast and powerful magnetic field which varies and oscillates as Jupiter revolves and Europa orbits. If Europa has a salty ocean, that will generate a separate magnetic field, because a salty ocean is conductive. The strength and orientation of these fields are always changing. There's also a large body of magnetospheric plasma that co-rotates with Jupiter at its magnetic equator, and its effects need to be accounted for, too. It's like a big, multi-faceted puzzle of magnetic fields that the Clipper's magnetometer is built to solve.

âThe magnetometer measures variations in the magnetic field as weâre orbiting Jupiter, but we need to pin these observations to something we know to understand the actual value that itâs measuring,â Pappalardo noted. âThe flyby will enable us to calibrate the instrument absolutely, using its observations at Earth to refine other calibrations done before launch and in flight.â.

Measuring Europa's magnetic field is also complicated because the Europa Clipper has its own unavoidable magnetic field. The spacecraft has more than 300 separate magnetic sources that its magnetometer must account for. Those range from magnets used in valves in its propellant system, to electrical current loops from its solar arrays. The magnetometer is mounted on a boom, called the Magboom, as far away from most of these sources as it can get, but it still needs to take them into consideration.

In a recent development, the Europa Clipper's magnetometer isn't its only important instrument. They're all important, or they wouldn't have survived the mission's rigorous design process. They'll all be active during the spacecraft's upcoming Earth flyby.

Industry observers note that the E-THEMIS (Europa Clipper Thermal Emission Imaging System) instrument will scan Earth every eight hours as the spacecraft approaches. Its purpose is to find hotspots on Europa's surface where water from its subsurface ocean may be closest to the surface, or even escaped above the ice. Then other remote-sensing instruments will follow up those observations. The MISE (Mapping Imaging Spectrometer for Europa) can examine that water and map its composition.

The Europa-UVS (Europa-Ultraviolet Spectrograph) will also scan Earth during the flyby. It's job is to to study Europa's surface and its atmosphere. It will compare its Earth observations to similar observations from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbit (LRO). When the Clipper is measuring Earth, the LRO will point at Earth and do the same with one of its instruments. Then the mission team can use both results to calibrate their instrument.

âItâs super-exciting when we actually do get to collect data thatâs really meaningful to the instruments, and get to share it with other people,â Leonard remarked. âThis is Earth, and everyone understands what that data means. Imagine what itâs going to be able to show you about Europa.â.

Industry observers note that the Europa Clipper is scheduled for a four-year mission at Jupiter. If there's no mission extension, then it will likely be crashed into Jupiter, Ganymede, or Callisto. NASA doesn't want to risk it crashing into Europa because of potential contamination. In 2022, Pappalardo suggested crashing it into Ganymede, because the ESA's Juice mission, which is also on its way to Jupiter, can observe that crash and use it to learn more about that moon's surface chemistry.

In a recent development, after this upcoming Earth flyby, the Europa Clipper will begin a long cruise phase. Not much happens during these cruise phases, which is good because it means nothing's gone wrong. Barring any significant problems, we may not hear much from the Europa Clipper until it reaches Jupiter in 2030.

Some time after that, we may finally get an answer to a long-burning question: Does Europa have a subsurface ocean with the right environment for life?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor to climate change, and it’s not even close. According to the United Nations, the industry is responsible for 68 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions and an incredible 90 percent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Stick a stake in the vampiric heart of fossil fuels, and beating back the worst effects of global warming becomes suddenly much more possible. But as the recent climate summit at Antalya, Türkiye, this month displayed, the industry highlights no interest in giving up its polluting ways, leading some countries to say the world is now “held hostage by the oil mafia.”.

Sources indicate that despite this unwillingness to change, some companies are trying to find ways to make some good out of a bad situation. One of those companies AIRCO (originally named Air Firm), based out of New Britain, Pennsylvania, did just that by developing a technology that creates jet fuel of a thin “air”—well, kind of.

Industry observers note that instead of making fuel at a massive refinery and transporting it long distances, the system is designed to produce fully formulated synthetic jet or diesel fuel closer to where it will be used,” Nick Steinke, the manufacturer’s director of programs, government and defense, said in a recent interview with Waste360. “It takes captured CO₂ and hydrogen and integrates the conversion process into a modular, containerized system.”.

Industry observers note that instead of relying on centralized fuel producers, the idea is that synthetic fuels could be created on-site where they’ll be used directly, circumventing the climate impacts of transporting the fuel entirely. Also the ingredients AIRCO uses also aims to come from green sources by leveraging carbon capture technologies for the required CO2 and using electrolysis to supply hydrogen from water.

It has been revealed that chemical & Engineering News reported earlier this year the manufacturer hopes to supply the U.S. military with a complete reactor system by 2027 that will be powered on a government site using a small nuclear reactor (SMR), and supply a sufficient flow of energy required for both carbon capture and electrolysis to provide the volumes of ingredients needed to make these mobile, fuel-creating systems viable. It’s a task that at least one expert says sounds easier said than done.

In a recent development, “The technology seems like it holds a lot of promise, especially on the fuel-conversion side, but the part that I have a lot of questions about is, where are you getting the carbon from?” Sarah Gleeson, a materials scientist at Project Drawdown, told WHYY, a local radio station. “Because if they’re saying that there’s some kind of direct air capture functionality in this really mobile device, I would be skeptical at the capacity and efficiency of it.”.

Carbon capture is central to the company’s promise of its technology’s carbon-neutral nature with the company’s CEO telling WHYY that “using more CO2 in our production process to make the fuel than we are putting out in the entire process.” Carbon capture, as a broad technology category, still remains unproved even as some climate models rely on its implementation (and the fact that the oil industry likes the technology is concerning to say the least).

If humanity hopes to secure a healthy planet for future generations, ending its reliance on fossil fuels is priority number one. But step one in the process is first limiting—and eventually eliminating— upcoming fuel from being extracted from the ground in the first place while the advancements in green chemistry try to put to work the carbon dioxide that’s already here.

Mathematicians Find a Brilliant Shortcut to a 174-Year-Old Math Puzzle

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A faster way to color maps using only four colors has revealed hidden mathematical patterns that could help solve puzzles involving far more complex shapes.
  • In a recent development, in 1852, English mathematician Francis Guthrie noticed something curious while drawing a map of England’s counties.
  • It has been revealed that what seemed like a simple observation became one of the most famous problems in mathematics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A faster way to color maps using only four colors has revealed hidden mathematical patterns that could help solve puzzles involving far more complex shapes.

In a recent development, in 1852, English mathematician Francis Guthrie noticed something curious while drawing a map of England’s counties. He needed only four colors to ensure that no two neighboring counties shared the same color. Could the same be true of every flat map, regardless of how complicated its borders were?

It has been revealed that what seemed like a simple observation became one of the most famous problems in mathematics. It took 124 years to prove Guthrie right and another half century to discover the most efficient way to assign those four colors. In solving the latter problem, an international team of mathematicians has uncovered something previously unknown about the mathematical structures underlying maps.

Industry observers note that the history of the Four Color Problem is filled with frustrated attempts. A proof presented in 1879 stood for 11 years before an error was discovered. When mathematicians finally succeeded in 1976, their proof was controversial because it relied heavily on computer calculations that were difficult for others to verify. A more accessible proof followed in 1997, although finding a suitable coloring for large maps remained computationally demanding.

“The previous proofs indicated that it is always possible to color a map using four colors. But they are not very good at actually finding the colors for each individual region on a map. The new algorithm is efficient and provides a much faster way of coloring,” says Professor Mikkel Thorup from the Department of Computer Science at the University of Copenhagen.

The achievement marks the first major breakthrough on the problem in nearly 30 years. The first part of the research paper was presented at FOCS’26, one of the world’s leading conferences in theoretical computer science, where it received the Best Paper Award.

Mathematicians can represent a flat map using what is known as a planar graph. Imagine replacing each country or county with a dot and drawing lines between those that share a border. The challenge then becomes assigning colors to the dots so that no two connected dots have the same color.

Recent findings suggest that within these graphs are small arrangements called reducible configurations, which allow mathematicians to simplify the coloring problem. The researchers discovered that graphs contain far more of these useful arrangements than anyone previously realized.

Industry observers note that “Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four coloring. We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before,” says Professor and co-author Carsten Thomassen from DTU.

Recent findings suggest that where earlier methods could often identify only one suitable starting point, the researchers can now work from many different parts of a graph. The advantage becomes particularly pronounced as maps grow larger.

“We have gone from what mathematicians call quadratic time to linear time. This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” explains Carsten Thomassen.

Recent findings suggest that finding this solution occupied Thorup and his colleagues, including Thomassen, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, and Bojan Mohar, for around a decade. Thorup has a name for the peculiar fascination that has kept mathematicians returning to the problem for 174 years: “the four-color disease.”.

“The disease is believing that there must be a simple proof for such a simple statement. I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding. It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”.

Thorup is equally candid about the appeal of devoting years to an apparently modest mathematical puzzle.

It has been revealed that “Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions. We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles,” states Mikkel Thorup.

It has been revealed that that possibility is already emerging from the team’s work. The abundance of reducible configurations could help mathematicians investigate more complex graphs and surfaces whose geometry differs considerably from that of an ordinary map.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map. For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of Emmental cheese. That is why we believe the result could have significance far beyond the Four Color Theorem,” notes Mikkel Thorup.

Reference: “The Four Color Theorem with Linearly Many Reducible Configurations and Near-Linear Time Coloring” by Yuta Inoue, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Atsuyuki Miyashita, Bojan Mohar, Carsten Thomassen and Mikkel Thorup, September 30, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2603.24880.

Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
  • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they noted old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they noted old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He remarked “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the complications were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin mentioned “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin noted the fresh $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin stated. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

Sources indicate that senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

In a recent development, the 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight looks. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

According to recent reports, the committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a newly introduced one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., stated in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications complications.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell remarked.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and stated their committee would “thoroughly review the challenges that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

Industry observers note that at issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

Astronomers Discover a Hidden Binary in a Star System Used to Calibrate the JWST

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when observatories like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) conduct observation campaigns, they often start by observing star fields to calibrate their instruments.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery was made by a team from the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), who found the binary while reviewing long-term observations from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS).
  • From the TESS data, the team noticed that HD 158485 was pulsing in six distinct rhythms, otherwise known as Î´ Scuti pulsation modes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when observatories like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) conduct observation campaigns, they often start by observing star fields to calibrate their instruments. These stars must have precisely characterized spectra so that their radiant energy (or fluxes) can be measured accurately. However, some stars that appear as single objects have a binary companion that has not been resolved, altering their predicted stellar flux. In fact, a star that is used for JWST calibration (HD 158485), which was thought to be an A-type star, has been identified as a binary system.

According to recent reports, the discovery was made by a team from the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), who found the binary while reviewing long-term observations from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, provides the first orbital solution and dynamical mass ratio for the system. HD 158485 is an example of a pulsating, variable, or Delta (Î´) Scuti star, which experiences brightness changes at a regular frequency (typically every 18 minutes to 8 hours).

From the TESS data, the team noticed that HD 158485 was pulsing in six distinct rhythms, otherwise known as Î´ Scuti pulsation modes. They further noticed that these pulses fell into two groups with opposing light-travel-time variations, meaning that the light from these pulses reached Earth at different times. This could only be explained by the presence of a binary companion. The team used the variation between the two signals to trace the star's orbital motion with HD 158485, which indicated that they orbit each other every 382.8 days.

Recent findings suggest that pulsation timing results for HD 158485. The two groups of pulsation modes show opposite time delays, revealing the orbital motion of both stars. Credit: Chenglong, LV et al. (2026).

The data also allowed them to constrain the orbital parameters and the star's mass. According to their calculations, the companion has an eccentricity of 0.242, indicating a moderately elongated, closed elliptical orbit, and is about 80% as massive as its primary - making it a likely F-type (yellow-white) main-sequence star. Their findings are independently confirmed by an orbital model built from earlier TESS data, which accurately predicted the timing variations that were detected by a separate observation campaign.

The team further compared a two-star atmosphere model with a conventional single-star model using the system's mass ratio, which showed a flux difference of about 1.6% between one and five micrometers (Î¼m), and 2.5% between five and 28 Î¼m. These findings could have significant implications where JWST calibration is concerned. While they do not represent a measured error, they do show how mistaking a binary system for a single star can shift predicted fluxes, thus throwing off readings.

Recent findings suggest that in essence, the team's results show that stellar pulsations can reveal binaries that conventional observations leave unresolved. It also underscores the need to account for hidden stellar companions when evaluating calibration standards for our instruments.

Further Reading: Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Why Some Farts Can Clear a Room While Others Barely Smell

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A microbiologist reveals the surprising gut chemistry behind room-clearing farts, why some stink more than others, and how their terrible smell may serve a useful purpose.
  • A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day.
  • In a recent development, farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A microbiologist reveals the surprising gut chemistry behind room-clearing farts, why some stink more than others, and how their terrible smell may serve a useful purpose.

A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. Altogether, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

In a recent development, farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an crucial job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

Industry observers note that as a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.

So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?

Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

Anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three-quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen, and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

According to recent reports, but wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

Sources indicate that one key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

It has been revealed that only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in Upcoming York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.

Your farts’ aroma depends on what your microbiome gets to eat.

The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Industry observers note that some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.

However, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

In a recent development, when you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

As you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

According to recent reports, farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness Book of World Records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mishears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

In a recent development, but sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

In a recent development, despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves, and volcanic vents that can suffocate and kill you.

So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

Recent findings suggest that written by Brenda A. Wilson, Professor of Microbiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

According to recent reports, A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. In a recent development, for those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. In a recent development, even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice manufacturer’s new holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

Sources indicate that when it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. It really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer.
