📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The last few days weâve been covering a series of papers by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory about the constraints surrounding the use of orbital data centers in space. One that has come up repeatedly is weight, and the solar panels used to power these data centers contribute a significant portion of that weight. So why not go with an alternative power source? Nuclear energy in space applications is having a bit of a moment right now â maybe it could provide the power needed for the orbital data center revolution? According to another paper from Dr. Turyshev, released as a preprint on arXiv, it all depends on the mission requirements.

One major problem with using solar panels for orbital data centers is the Sun doesnât always shine in their orbit. During some seasons, each orbital pass will result in the satellite crossing over the Earthâs shadow for up to 21 minutes. And given that the orbits these data centers are on happen around 15 times each day, that means in a 24-hour day, the satellite spends around 5 hours and 13 minutes in the Earth's shadow.

Industry observers note that to combat this problem, engineers turn to an obvious solution â batteries. But they are notorious for being heavy, and according to Dr. Turyshevâs calculations, providing enough storage capacity to combat a 21-minute stretch with no power, would require a 1 MW data center cluster to haul 6.46 metric tons of batteries into orbit. Combine that with the needed solar panels and radiators to get rid of waste heat as infrared light, and you end up with a total mass of 43 metric tons for a 1 MW cluster, even before counting any actual computing hardware.

Fraser talks about the potential of a nuclear reactor in space.

A fission reactor would eliminate the need for solar wings, as well as batteries. However, it doesnât really deal well with the other physical constraint on these systems â waste heat. While it eliminates the heat generated by the solar panels themselves, it introduces another engineering problem â getting rid of the heat at two different temperatures.

Industry observers note that running a nuclear fission reactor at 25% efficiency (which is pretty standard for thermal electrical conversion) would produce about 3 megawatts of conversion waste heat for every one megawatt of energy generated, meaning a one-megawatt computing cluster creates nearly four megawatts of ultra-hot waste heat from its power conversion machinery alone. This waste heat would be at around 700 Kelvin â more than double the maximum temperature that processors on the data centers need to be kept below in order not to fry themselves. While this higher-temperature heat can be radiated away with a relatively compact radiator, it would have to be separate from the thermal sinks cooling the processors below their 320 Kelvin ideal temperature. Ultimately, a nuclear-powered cluster would only need around 6% less low temperature radiator area than a fully solar-powered version.

Recent findings suggest that despite that, after adding all the mass of the reactor, radiation shielding, power converters, and all the other necessary equipment to run a nuclear reactor, fission originally looks like a winner. Compared to todayâs standard solar panels, a compact fission reactor is around ten metric tons lighter per megawatt. And since weight is money in space, that sounds like a win.

Fraser talks about the fresh nuclear reactor NASA will use for future Mars missions.

However, there are several caveats to that. First, lighter, next-generation solar arrays are coming along swiftly, whose increased efficiency could eliminate nuclearâs advantage entirely. Or the engineers could boost the satelliteâs orbit up to 1,450 kilometers, where the Earthâs shadow problem completely goes away and the satellite can consistently bathe in sunlight â admittedly ignoring the potential space debris and trapped radiation problems this causes, as well as the need for higher power communications equipment.

Nuclear suffers from another disadvantage - radiation. Data centers in space already suffer from stray cosmic rays flipping bits unexpectedly. Putting one next to an active nuclear reactor subjects them to random gamma rays and neutrons as well. While this could be lessened a bit by putting the reactor on a long boom â physically separating it from the server racks and placing a dense âshadow shieldâ near the reactor to block radiation from reaching the computers, that would require extra weight in the form of cabling and the boom itself, eliminating more of nuclearâs original weight advantage.

According to recent reports, despite all these trade-offs, there does appear to be a situation where running a hybrid of both solar and nuclear is the best option. If a mission requires a data center to survive a 24-hour failure of its main power system while keeping 20% emergency power active for safe-mode operation, an 80/20 nuclear/solar split weighs in at around 36 metric tons, around a third of the weight of either as a standalone option due to the weight of batteries needed to meet those mission requirements. But to be clear, without that power maintenance constraint, either system in a standalone configuration wins out on weight.

Fraser talks aobut the advantages and disadvantages of orbital data centers.

Industry observers note that ultimately, Dr. Turyshev thinks the financial picture is dependent on the lifespan of the nuclear reactor. Another disadvantage of a nuclear-powered satellite is it canât just burn up in the atmosphere at the end of its life â it has to be boosted to a âgraveyardâ orbit at around 2,000 km, where a spent reactor would stay indefinitely. But, if a reactor lasts ten years, Dr. Turyshev calculates that it would save around $190 per kilowatt-year in launch costs, whereas if it lasts for only two years (as many experimental space-based reactors are designed to), then that flips to a $783 per kilowatt-year deficit.

What the paper doesnât tackle is the social aspect of whether the general public would support putting potentially tens of thousands of small nuclear reactors into orbit. Just this week, NASA and the U.S. Department of Energy locked in the mission architecture for a nuclear-powered reactor known as Space Reactor-1 Freedom to power the propulsion system of a future Mars mission, so thereâs at least some support for it (or at least the government thinks there is). But as more and more data centers are launched, how to power them with the best trade-off of weight vs cost vs safety vs capability will remain an ongoing debate.

#170236. Scientists Discover Strange Dinosaur That Evolved To Eat Fruit

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (809 w)

Scientists Discover Strange Dinosaur That Evolved To Eat Fruit

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dinosaur’s resemblance to modern fruit-eating parrots offers clues to how prehistoric animals adapted as flowering plants transformed life on land.
  • In a recent development, as flowering plants spread across the Cretaceous landscape, fruits became larger and more abundant, offering dinosaurs an entirely different source of food.
  • It has been revealed that the newly identified species, Infernogallus jamesi, is the first known dinosaur with anatomical adaptations specifically linked to fruit consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dinosaur’s resemblance to modern fruit-eating parrots offers clues to how prehistoric animals adapted as flowering plants transformed life on land.

In a recent development, as flowering plants spread across the Cretaceous landscape, fruits became larger and more abundant, offering dinosaurs an entirely different source of food. Paleontologists have long struggled to understand how this transformation influenced dinosaur evolution. Now, the discovery of a turkey-sized dinosaur that lived alongside T. rex suggests that some dinosaurs developed remarkably sophisticated ways of eating fruit, much like parrots do today.

It has been revealed that the newly identified species, Infernogallus jamesi, is the first known dinosaur with anatomical adaptations specifically linked to fruit consumption. The discovery was made by researchers from Stony Brook University, the Royal Ontario Museum (ROM), and the North Dakota Geological Survey. Led by Dr. Gregory Funston, assistant professor in the Department of Anatomical Sciences at Stony Brook University, the study was published in Nature Communications.

It has been revealed that “We knew dinosaurs evolved to fill so many different roles in ecosystems in the Cretaceous, but we never expected to discover fruit-eating dinosaurs,” notes Dr. Gregory Funston. “For more than 100 years, we didn’t know what the skulls of these animals looked like. Now, we know they were even weirder than we could have predicted.”.

Recent findings suggest that the dinosaur’s name, Infernogallus, means “hell chicken,” a reference to the Hell Creek Formation where its fossils were discovered. The formation stretches across Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Wyoming and preserves remains of familiar dinosaurs such as T. rex and Triceratops, which lived alongside Infernogallus. Its nearly complete skull, with the bones still connected, and partial skeleton are presently on display at the Royal Ontario Museum.

Despite descending from meat-eating dinosaurs, Infernogallus belonged to a group of toothless, feathered oviraptorosaurs known as caenagnathids. Weighing approximately 25 pounds (12 kilograms) as a fully grown adult, it was one of the smallest members of its group.

“It’s pretty rare for animals to become specialized for a diet of fruit, so when it happens, it comes with some remarkable adaptations,” claims Dr. Thomas Dudgeon, Rebanks Postdoctoral Research Fellow at ROM and a co-author of the study. “The anatomy of Infernogallus is bizarre among dinosaurs, and we swiftly realized that we were dealing with something special.”.

In a recent development, using CT scans to reconstruct the skull, the researchers noticed something unusual about the bones forming the roof of the mouth. These bones curved downward into the mouth, positioning certain chewing muscles horizontally rather than vertically. Instead of relying on the rigid, up-and-down bite characteristic of dinosaurs such as T. rex, Infernogallus could have moved its beak back and forth in a chewing motion similar to our own.

According to recent reports, forward-facing chewing muscles are uncommon in the animal kingdom, although they occur in mammals capable of complex chewing and in certain fruit-eating birds. The particular muscle arrangement identified in Infernogallus resembles that of the modern vulturine parrot (Psittrichas), suggesting that the dinosaur was adapted to processing soft food in its mouth rather than its gut. Its chewing motion appears to have been especially suited to separating the flesh of stone fruits from their hard central pits.

According to recent reports, the finding also reveals an intriguing parallel in evolutionary history. As fruits became larger and more common, caenagnathids developed increasingly specialized chewing capabilities.

Fossilized fruits document how flowering plants gradually replaced cone-bearing plants as the dominant vegetation on land during the Cretaceous. By eating fruit, dinosaurs may have helped disperse seeds and influenced the evolution of flowering plants, fulfilling an ecological role that birds, reptiles, and small mammals play today.

“Complete remains of small dinosaurs like Infernogallus are very rare in the fossil record. The strange skull of Infernogallus is an exciting find because it reveals surprising insights into dinosaur evolution and feeding specialization,” claims Dr. David Evans, chief curator of natural history and Temerty Chair in Vertebrate Paleontology at ROM and senior author of the paper. “This discovery highlights that we still have a lot to learn about the world of T. rex, and about dinosaurs more generally.”.

Industry observers note that the discovery also contributes to an ongoing debate over whether dinosaurs were already in decline before their extinction. The specialized feeding behavior of Infernogallus suggests that the diversity of dinosaurs, and the ecological roles they occupied near the end of the Cretaceous, may have been greater than the fossil record has so far revealed.

It has been revealed that reference: “Fruit-eating adaptations in a Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur (Theropoda)” by Gregory F. Funston, Thomas W. Dudgeon, D. Jade Simon, Danielle M. Dufault, Clint Boyd, Denver Fowler, Philip J. Currie and David C. Evans, 10 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78343-w.

Sources indicate that studies show that in addition to STEM literacy, robotics can help develop core skills like hands-on creativity, problem solving, communication, and teamwork. Industry observers note that choose toys that allow your kid to use their imagination and play out multiple different situations, both real and made up. The ESO is Deeply Concerned About Space Data Centers, and the Rest of Us Should Be Too

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's growing concern that AI is polluting our communal spaces.
  • According to recent reports, there's also growing concern that AI, or at least its infrastructure, is taking over physical spaces.
  • And the potential loss of privacy, loss of freedom, and the spectre of a growing surveillance regime stemming from AI isn't helping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's growing concern that AI is polluting our communal spaces. AI is replacing humans online, and we wonder if there's another human being behind what we're reading or viewing. We wonder where this will go, and how it will end.

According to recent reports, there's also growing concern that AI, or at least its infrastructure, is taking over physical spaces. Data centers are proliferating, and citizens are concerned about their effects: power usage, water usage, noise, etc. The promise of a few jobs isn't placating concerns about what some say are resource-hogging data centers being forced on communities despite their opposition.

And the potential loss of privacy, loss of freedom, and the spectre of a growing surveillance regime stemming from AI isn't helping.

It has been revealed that but now AI data centers are about to take their place in the sky, the last frontier of communal space. This is setting off alarm bells for astronomers, who are adamant that the growing cloud of satellites is taking a serious toll on their observations.

Industry observers note that the FCC just approved SpaceX's application to launch a staggering one million new satellites in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO). Together, they will be the first orbital AI data center. The system is designed to avoid using energy and resources here on Earth. The satellites will operate in nearly constant sunlight for solar power, and will cool themselves by pumping liquid coolant through radiative panels. The individual satellites would stay in constant contact with each other with lasers.

With Musk/SpaceX's typical hubris, they're calling the system 'Starmind.'.

But whatever they're calling it, not everyone is pleased that it's been approved, and many are questioning why the FCC, a purely American body, can be allowed to approve such a project.

It has been revealed that there are really two parallel problems. One is the growing number of satellites overall, and the other concerns the proliferation of AI.

This artist's illustration indicates the ESO's Extremely Large Telescope in the Atacama Desert in Chile. It's a 39 meter behemoth that will drive astronomical discoveries for decades. But a sky crowded with satellites will make its life difficult. Image Credit: ESO/L. CalÃ§ada.

Sources indicate that the European Southern Observatory (ESO) has made their thoughts known on the proliferation of satellites and how it affects astronomy. The ESO operates some of the most powerful existing and upcoming telescopes in the world in the Atacama Desert in Chile: The Very Large Telescope (VLT), the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the ESO 3.6-metre Telescope, and the ESO's upcoming flagship telescope, the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT).

In a newly introduced statement, the ESO condemns the Starmind project as a serious detriment to astronomical observations. And, unlike some other opponents, they've analyzed the situation in detail.

In a recent development, âAs approved, this project would not only have profound consequences for astronomy, but also fundamentally alter the night sky for everyone on the planet. We demonstrated these impacts in an extensive technical analysis, and raised them in a response to the US FCC, as did other organisations worldwide. This approval highlights the urgent need for international mechanisms capable of assessing activities whose impacts extend far beyond national borders and affect a global common good,â noted Andreas Kaufer, Director General at the European Southern Observatory (ESO).

Their technical analysis is peer-reviewed and was published in Astronomy and Astrophysics in March 2026.

According to recent reports, "Large satellite constellations impact astronomy through both visible trails and the generation of diffuse and atmospherically scattered light. Quantification of this cumulative sky-background component is essential to assess the full ramifications of extant and proposed systems," the paper states.

Recent findings suggest that these panels show the effect of one million satellites (V500km = 6), representing the SpaceX Orbital Data Center constellation in slight violation of the V > 7 recommendation. (a) highlights the fraction of the Field of View lost for the LSST camera at the Vera Rubin Observatory. (b) shows example positions of individual satellites. The grey dots represent invisible satellites in the Earthâs shadow, whereas the coloured dots represent illuminated satellites. The 1867 orange dots correspond to satellites brighter than V = 7, and the 247 red dots to satellites brighter than V = 5. For comparison, about 3000â4000 stars are this bright. Image Credit: Hainaut 2026. A&A Volume 712, August 2026 A241.

"This study evaluates the effect of proposed constellations â ranging from current deployments to mega-constellations and very bright reflector concepts â on direct trail losses, diffuse background, and scattered sky brightness.".

Constellations with up to about 60,000 member satellites have a negligible, but not imperceptible, effect on observations. But above that number, things change for the worse. "Conversely, mega-constellations with 106 satellites render trails pervasive, thereby affecting the majority of long exposures," they write. Long exposures are critical in modern astronomy, so the astronomers are taking the problem seriously.

It has been revealed that this figure illustrates the effect SpaceXâs one-million-satellite Orbital Data Center constellation on a 300-second exposure with the spectrograph at the Very Large Telescope. Even 1.3 h after the end of astronomical twilight, more than half the sky remains affected by satellite streaks, with an average of more than eight satellite trails per image at zenith. In some observations, more than 20 satellite trails will cross each image. The effect on a 15-second exposure with the 3Â° LSST camera at the Rubin observatory is similar. Image Credit: Hainaut 2026. A&A Volume 712, August 2026 A241.

Long exposures are especially important when observing high-redshift objects or other faint objects. High-resolution spectroscopy and deep-time surveys also use long exposures. Astronomical telescopes can take short exposures and stack them to deal with some satellite light-streak pollution, but that has its limits.

"Bright satellites, such as spacecraft analogous to AST SpaceMobile, significantly impact saturating detectors even when their number is moderate. Extremely bright satellites pose a far more severe threat: a 5000-satellite Reflect Orbital-like constellation could elevate the scattered sky background by 20â30%, and a population of 50 000 could increase it by 200â300%," the ESO paper states.

The ESO's technical analysis mentioned there are current proposals to launch 1.7 million latest satellites into space, and many of them breach a critical threshold called V550km = 7. That figure indicates a satellite that can't be seen with the naked eye, so breaching that figure means it can be seen with the naked eye. That means that not only will we see them when we gaze upward, but astronomical telescope observations would be inundated with them. The ESO's analysis says dryly that they "would substantially degrade astronomical observations.".

"Maintaining satellite brightness below V550km = 7 is vital for all instruments but critical for safeguarding saturating instruments, such as the Rubin LSST camera, and for limiting sky-background pollution," the paper states.

In a recent development, reflect Orbital has something other than AI or communications in mind. They intend to launch large reflecting satellites into orbit. Those satellites would reflect sunlight to customers on the ground. They could illuminate solar panel farms at night, or provide light to allow things like resource extraction to continue past nightfall. But things can always go wrong. Think of hackers or other malicious actors gaining control of an orbiting light source.

But the real problem astronomers face from Reflect Orbital is that their satellites would blow past the V550km = 7 threshold.

In a recent development, this figure demonstrates scattered light as a fraction of the natural dark sky for 37 (a), 5000 (b), and 50 000 (c) extremely bright satellites (V500km = â4), representing the Reflect Orbital constellations envisaged for 2027, 2030, and 2035, respectively, as seen from outside their illuminating beam. Image Credit: Hainaut 2026. A&A Volume 712, August 2026 A241.

Industry observers note that reflect Orbital's eventual 2035 constellation of 50,000 bright satellites would be catastrophic for the Vera Rubin and its LSST. "For the saturating LSST Camera, however, the effects of even a single satellite crossing its FoV will be devastating, compromising a very high fraction of the frame affected by that single trail. The 2030 constellation (5000 satellites) would ruin 3% (at zenith) to 12% (at 30Â° elevation) of the LSST FoV one hour after sunset. With the 2035 constellation (50 000 satellites), the losses would be catastrophic, about 30% at zenith to 100% at 30Â°: all LSST images would be entirely unusable," the ESO's paper states.

Sources indicate that these panels show the fraction of exposures captured by the LSST that will be unusable because of Reflect Orbital's satellites. (a) is for 36 satellites in 2027, (b) is for 5,000 satellites in 2030, and (c) is for 50,000 satellites in 2035.

"Even under this constraint, the total satellite population should remain below â¼100 000 satellites to ensure that field-of-view losses do not exceed typical technical downtime," they state.

Companies like SpaceX aren't blind to the problem. They're trying to make their satellites less reflective. But their impact on astronomy is just one outcome of the ongoing crowding of LEO. What about the proliferation of space junk? There are efforts to develop ways of mitigating the space junk problem, but they're way behind the massive number of satellites being rolled out. SpaceX says they have a proposal, and the FCC approves it, but the plan is really just disposal by atmospheric re-entry.

Most people aren't too concerned with astronomical observations, except when one makes the news headlines. But some are concerned about reflecting sunlight down onto Earth at night as a business model. For astronomers, it could be catastrophic.

According to recent reports, far more people are concerned with AI intruding where they don't think it belongs. Do we really need AI in space?

Some are saying that Starmind will never be built, that it's part of the SpaceX/Elon Musk hype machine. But those are just some of the opinions out there, and they don't touch on regular citizens' concerns about the encroachment of AI and its infrastrcture into their lives.

Recent findings suggest that besides, SpaceX isn't the only organization contemplating a satellite AI data processing system. Blue Origin is also considering an orbital data center satellite system. It's called Project Sunrise and would have 51,000 satellites.

Recent findings suggest that we've been warned about the growing number of satellites for years now. In a 2021 paper, researchers warned us about the danger associated with "the adoption of a consumer electronic model applied to space assets." Consumer electronics are creating mountains of electronic waste that we're struggling to manage. The proliferation of satellites is adding to our pollution problem.

It has been revealed that in the 2021 paper, the authors point out that "satellite re-entries from the Starlink mega-constellation alone could deposit more aluminum into Earthâs upper atmosphere than what is done through meteoroids; they could thus become the dominant source of high-altitude alumina." High-altitude alumina is bad because it may trigger chemical reactions that destroy ozone. And the alumina isn't destroyed itself, so it could drive multiple cycles of ozone destruction.

According to recent reports, this image is a 333 second-exposure from the Blanco 4-meter telescope at the Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory. It reveals at least 19 streaks created by the second batch of Starlink satellites rolled out in November 2019. Image Credit: NSFâs National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory/CTIO/AURA/DELVE, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Crowding LEO with more satellites is fraught with problems. But our rapid and widespread adoption of AI in particular could be especially dangerous. AI data centers in space combine both problems into one. Implementing satellite AI systems may end up being a very bad decision, maybe humanity's last massive, bad decision.

Sources indicate that who knows where this will go, and who knows if AI is going to destroy humanity. That type of thinking used to sound like an exaggerated science fiction nightmare, or an easily-dismissed, feverish thought experiment. But many AI experts say we're heading for trouble, we're moving too fast, and we're not building in safeguards. The people who build AI can't actually explain how it works. We all know about AI hallucinating and inventing facts, but AI has been caught scheming and deceiving, behaving one way outwardly while hiding its true intentions. That's truly alarming.

There's no denying that AI is a powerful tool. It's powering scientific discoveries and it's helping regular people every day. But that's just one side of it.

According to recent reports, from a POTUSA who posted an AI video of himself wrestling a tigerâshortly after a real person was unfortunately killed by oneâto armies of bots spreading political misinformation designed to undermine a nation's sovereignty, to financial scammers with a global reach, AI's presence is proving to be toxic. It ranges from mildly problematic to outright hostile. Bad actors are rapidly adopting this new, powerful tool, and using it to harmful effect.

In a recent development, it's amost impossible to deny that we're on the cusp of something historic. Humanity always struggles with new powerful tools because wisdom lags behind intelligence. It always has and it always will; the only way to acquire wisdom is through experience. Do we have enough wisdom to make careful decisions regarding AI?

At different times in history, angry mobs of citizens have been the only thing standing in the way of terrible ideas and actions. To place AI in space, beyond the reach of the angry mob and its pitchforks, may end up being a terrible mistake.

According to recent reports, A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a major baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

Those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

It has been revealed that “There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling.

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World.

Recent findings suggest that “I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the major stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen.

“We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking.

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash.

According to recent reports, “I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most important one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

It has been revealed that “Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World.

Industry observers note that “We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya.

Ancient Bison Hunting Site in Texas Challenges Decades of Archaeological Assumptions

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Evidence of communal bison hunts spanning 3,000 years in Texas offers a fascinating glimpse into the enduring knowledge and ingenuity of ancient Indigenous hunter-gatherers.
  • Industry observers note that for Indigenous hunter-gatherers in the Southern Plains, a successful large-scale bison hunt likely depended on people performing different jobs across the landscape.
  • In a recent development, archaeologists have now uncovered evidence that generations of Indigenous communities carried out such hunts at the same location in the Texas Panhandle over approximately 3,000 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evidence of communal bison hunts spanning 3,000 years in Texas offers a fascinating glimpse into the enduring knowledge and ingenuity of ancient Indigenous hunter-gatherers.

Industry observers note that for Indigenous hunter-gatherers in the Southern Plains, a successful large-scale bison hunt likely depended on people performing different jobs across the landscape. Some hunters located herds and guided them toward grazing areas near a cliff, while others waited in hiding to drive the animals over the edge, where the fall would kill or incapacitate them. Additional teams would have killed injured bison and processed the meat, hides, and other materials.

In a recent development, archaeologists have now uncovered evidence that generations of Indigenous communities carried out such hunts at the same location in the Texas Panhandle over approximately 3,000 years. Known as Nighthawk, the site lies within Caprock Canyons State Park and is only the second scientifically verified example of a bison jump in Texas. For decades, archaeologists had questioned whether this sophisticated hunting technique, widely documented in the northern Great Plains, was also practiced farther south.

The findings, published in the journal American Antiquity, come from a collaborative investigation involving the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, Texas Tech University, Plains Archeological Research, and other research partners. Rice University adjunct lecturer August “Gus” Costa served as a principal investigator and is the study’s lead author.

It has been revealed that “Bison jumping is exciting because it’s a community activity,” Costa noted. “Large-scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful.”.

These gatherings likely fulfilled needs beyond securing food and other resources. Costa believes the hunts provided opportunities for communities to trade, hold ceremonies, celebrate, and strengthen social relationships.

Initially, stone spear and arrow points recovered at Nighthawk suggested that at least two hunts had taken place there. Radiocarbon dating of bison bones revealed a much longer history, identifying evidence of at least seven separate hunting events spanning approximately three millennia.

During that time, hunting technology shifted from stone-tipped spears to bows and arrows, pottery was introduced, and the surrounding landscape underwent substantial changes. Erosion alone moved the cliff’s jump-off point roughly the length of a football field.

“Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility,” Costa said.

In a recent development, the shape of the landscape also presents an intriguing problem. At many northern Plains bison jumps, the terrain may have concealed the cliff edge from approaching animals. Nighthawk, however, sits on a projecting cliff, meaning the bison could likely see the danger ahead. How hunters adapted their methods to overcome this difficulty remains unknown.

“We don’t know exactly how they managed herding the bison, but the setting is different from the typical northern Plains jump,” Costa remarked.

Before Nighthawk was documented, Bonfire Shelter, identified more than 60 years ago, was the only scientifically verified bison jump in Texas. Costa and his colleagues have since identified eight additional potential sites in and around Caprock Canyons, suggesting that the practice may have been considerably more widespread.

According to recent reports, part of the difficulty in finding these sites lies in where archaeologists traditionally look. Investigations often concentrate on former living areas, where people left tools and other traces of daily life. Steep slopes beneath cliffs would have made poor campsites and consequently received less attention. Erosion and limited access to private property have further complicated the search.

“The jump was hidden in plain sight,” Costa remarked.

With fieldwork at Nighthawk complete, the researchers are searching for additional sites across the Southern Plains. They are also examining ancient bison DNA and the chemical composition of bones and teeth to reconstruct herd migrations, understand past environmental conditions, and investigate possible connections to the bison living in Caprock Canyons State Park today.

“For a long time when it comes to Indigenous bison hunting culture, the Southern Plains hasn’t received much respect, at least when compared to the north,” Costa said.

Industry observers note that for Costa, the discovery illustrates the danger of judging ancient societies solely by the evidence that happens to survive. Gaps in the archaeological record can obscure generations of accumulated knowledge, ingenuity, and cultural practices.

In a recent development, “It’s about respect,” Costa stated. “Bison jumping is a complicated community effort, and getting that incorporated into the story of Southern Plains people is important.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “The Nighthawk Bison Jump: New Evidence for Recurrent Late Holocene Bison Jumping in the Southern Plains” by August G. Costa, Brett A. Houk, Anthony S. Lyle, Leland Bement, Christopher Lintz, Ken L. Lawrence, Charles D. Frederick and Brendan J. Culleton, 9 November 2026, American Antiquity. DOI: 10.1017/aaq.2026.10229.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when astronomers look out into the Milky Way at very young stars, they find rings in their protoplanetary disks.
  • In a recent development, ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, has captured images of many of these disks and rings.
  • Industry observers note that âThese latest stars have bright rings and dark gaps patterned in concentric circles resembling the grooves of a vinyl record,â mentioned Masayuki Yamaguchi, a post-Doctoral Fellow from Kyushu Universityâs Faculty of Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when astronomers look out into the Milky Way at very young stars, they find rings in their protoplanetary disks. It's pretty clear that these rings are where planets are forming. They're carving gaps and rings in the protoplanetary disks, the reservoirs of material around stars that planets form from.

In a recent development, ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, has captured images of many of these disks and rings. Those images are part of the effort to understand how planets form, one of the primary questions in contemporary astronomy. But it's not clear if every ring is because of a planet. Protoplanetary disks are complex, and there are many forces at work in them. Some rings could be planets, and some could be caused by other phenomena.

Industry observers note that âThese latest stars have bright rings and dark gaps patterned in concentric circles resembling the grooves of a vinyl record,â mentioned Masayuki Yamaguchi, a post-Doctoral Fellow from Kyushu Universityâs Faculty of Science. âThese patterns arenât new; what was a mystery was how these grooves were carved. The most popular explanation is that young planets make these gaps as they orbit the star. However, when a disk has many rings, it becomes harder to explain since itâs hard to imagine that multiple planets have already formed.â.

Sources indicate that yamaguchi is the lead author of latest research in The Astrophysical Journal titled "A Hybrid Origin for the Multiple Ring-gap Structures in the Large Protoplanetary Disk V1094 Sco: A Low-mass Planet and Secular Gravitational Instability" Yamaguchi is a member of a team of Japanese astronomers who studied V1094 Scorpii, a young star about 500 light years away. V1094 Sco has a protoplanetary disk that extends out to 300 astronomical units, with multiple ring-gap pairs at great distances from the star.

According to recent reports, this is ALMA's image of V1094 Sco reconstructed with PRIISM. The researchers detected rings and gaps in the disk and were able to determine which were from still-forming planets. Image Credit: By YMasayuki - Own work, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/194635370.

"High spatial resolution observations reveal that some protoplanetary disks host multiple ringâgap pairs at large stellocentric radii, yet their physical origin remains unsettled," the authors write. The researchers used ALMA images and observations with the Very Large Telescope's SPHERE (Spectro-Polarimetric High-contrast Exoplanet REsearch) instrument to analyze the V1094 Sco disk. "The continuum image highlights four narrow dust ringâgap pairs extending to exceptionally large radii (r â¼ 380 au)," they write, and also "trace a spatially extended gas disk (r â¼ 760 au) in Keplerian rotation." Keplerian rotation means that objects further from the star orbit slower than those nearer the star.

Recent findings suggest that young stars with protoplanetary disks are T-Tauri stars, and among that group, V1094 Sco is known for having a giant disk with multiple rings, making it a rarity. It's the subject of a lot of research and observations. It was first recognized for its extended ring with multiple gaps and rings in a 2018 paper. That paper said, "In this work, the nature of V1094 Sco as a giant, multi-ringed protoplanetary disk is identified for the first time, based on data from the Lupus survey of protoplanetary disks." (The Lupus survey was an ALMA survey of disks in the Lupus star-forming complex.).

In a recent development, ever since then, astronomers have been trying to understand V1094 and its unusual disk. There's not much doubt that still-forming planets are responsible for some of its features, but can they explain them all?

In an interesting twist, the researchers didn't use new ALMA observing time to study V1094 Sco. They relied on existing data and applied a new open-source super-resolution imaging technique called PRIISM (Python module for Radio Interferometry Imaging with Sparse Modeling.) It was built specifically to reconstruct sharper images with existing ALMA data, and replaces a previous technique called CLEAN. PRIISM proved its value in a 2025 study of 78 disks in the Ophiuchus star-forming region, where it found previously undetectable features in disks, only a few hundred thousand years after the stars formed.

Recent findings suggest that this figure doesn't show V1094 Sco; instead it shows CrA IRS 2, a protostar about 430 light years away. It illustrates how much better PRIISM is at detecting disk structures in existing ALMA data than its predecessor, CLEAN. Image Credit: Ayumu Shoshi et al 2026 ApJ 998 214.

PRIISM paid similar dividends in this work.

âWe observed that the disk extends approximately 380 astronomical units (AU)âabout 13 times the distance between the Sun and Neptuneâfrom the center. Within that, we found four narrow rings and gaps between 100â230 AU from the starâs center,â explained Yamaguchi. âWhen we compared the widths and depths of the gaps with the "one planet per gap" model, we could not explain the entire pattern. Instead, the origin appears to differ from place to place.".

"The ensemble of gap widths and depths is inconsistent with a simple one-planet-per-gap interpretation," the authors write in their paper.

In a recent development, an exoplanet can explain the innermost gap, according to the results. "At r â 100 au, a double gap and its scattered-light counterpart are consistent with multigap excitation by a single low-mass companion of (55 Â± 35) Mâ," the authors explain.

But further from the disks, the rings were spaced more evenly. "At r â 170â230 au, the outer ring system indicates regular spacing and no clear scattered-light counterpart," the authors write. "These outer rings are quantitatively compatible with secular gravitational instability." That means the outer rings aren't associated with exoplanets. Instead, they're dust clumping together under its own gravity, which requires low turbulence.

Recent findings suggest that this is a near-infrared scattered-light image of the V1094 Sco disk obtained with VLT/SPHERE. It's overlain with the locations of dust continuum rings (solid lines) and gaps (dashed lines). The filled white circle indicates the SPHERE coronagraph. Image Credit: Masayuki Yamaguchi et al 2026 ApJ 1006 232.

Secular gravitational instability intrinsically produces evenly spaced rings, while exoplanets don't.

"V1094 Sco therefore supports a hybrid pathway in which weak turbulence in an extended disk allows secular gravitational instability to assemble long-lived midplane dust concentrations that can cradle planet formation beyond â¼100 au, alongside planet-driven substructures at intermediate radii," the authors write.

These results don't mean that planets won't eventually form in these features that are at great distances from the star. It just means that there are no planets forming there right now. "In this framework, secular GI does not compete with planet formation; rather, it concentrates solids and establishes disk-wide conditions favorable for subsequent planet growth," the authors write in their conclusion.

ALMA doesn't image planets; that was never its job. But if exoplanets are in V1094 Sco's disk, other telescopes might find them.

According to recent reports, âBecause ALMA is a radio telescope, we have not yet directly detected the planet that generates the gap closest to the star. Using other telescopes such as the Subaru Telescope will help us get a clearer picture of this hidden planet,â noted Yamaguchi. âAs we analyze more disks, our understanding of the fundamental question of where and how planets form will deepen. Each new finding adds a thread to the tapestry of our knowledge of the universe.â.

Alzheimer’s Breakthrough? Experimental Nose Drops Restore Youthful Memory in Mice

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Experimental nose drops helped mice with signs of Alzheimer’s hold on to their memory, even though the treatment left the brain’s telltale protein clumps in place.
  • What if some of the memory loss associated with aging could be reversed with something as simple as nose drops?
  • In a recent development, scientists at the University of Sydney have taken a promising step toward that possibility, developing an experimental treatment that restored learning and memory performance in older mice to levels comparable to those of younger animals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Experimental nose drops helped mice with signs of Alzheimer’s hold on to their memory, even though the treatment left the brain’s telltale protein clumps in place.

What if some of the memory loss associated with aging could be reversed with something as simple as nose drops?

In a recent development, scientists at the University of Sydney have taken a promising step toward that possibility, developing an experimental treatment that restored learning and memory performance in older mice to levels comparable to those of younger animals. The same approach also protected mice genetically predisposed to Alzheimer’s-like disease from cognitive decline.

In a recent development, both experiments centered on brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a protein that helps nerve cells survive and adjust their connections as memories form. Lower levels of BDNF are associated with aging and Alzheimer’s disease. Supplying the brain with more of the protein poses a familiar problem. The blood-brain barrier keeps many medicines in the bloodstream from reaching brain tissue. Connections between the nasal cavity and the brain offer another way in, without surgery or injections into the brain or spinal cord.

“If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer’s that bypasses the blood-brain barrier,” said Professor Greg Neely, whose lab at the university’s Charles Perkins Centre led the study.

In a recent development, the researchers adapted the clinically validated design of the messenger RNA (mRNA) used in BioNTech’s COVID-19 vaccine, where it carries instructions that prompt an immune response. For the nose drops, the team packaged mRNA carrying instructions for BDNF in tiny particles made of fats, called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). As the researchers reported in Advanced Science, cells in the nose read those instructions and made the protein, which could then reach the brain.

Sources indicate that “The success of mRNA vaccines indicated these systems can safely deliver genetic instructions to cells,” stated first author Dr. Maria Bergamasco of the university’s School of Life and Environmental Sciences. “We wanted to see whether we could adapt that technology to deliver beneficial proteins to the brain in a completely non-invasive way.”.

To compare older and younger mice, the researchers used standardized behavioral tests that measured how well the animals could hold information in mind briefly, remember places, and recognize objects.

“In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime,” Neely stated. “What’s exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic.”.

Sources indicate that for the Alzheimer’s experiment, the team used 5XFAD mice, a “humanized” model in which genetic mutations cause signs of the disease to appear rapidly. The researchers gave the mice nose drops twice a week starting at two months of age, when the first changes in the brain are usually detectable. At four months, when these mice typically begin to lose cognitive abilities, the treated animals showed no further decline.

Industry observers note that the researchers also saw more latest neurons forming in the hippocampus, a brain region critical for learning and memory. In the Alzheimer’s model, the drops preserved brain function without reducing amyloid plaques, the clumps of protein that are a hallmark of the disease.

Recent findings suggest that “Current Alzheimer’s treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques,” Neely noted. “However just under a third of Alzheimer’s patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it’s possible to live with Alzheimer’s disease pathology.”.

It has been revealed that “Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other.”.

According to recent reports, the researchers think the nasal delivery system could eventually carry medicines for stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental diseases. “This is a very exciting proof of concept for a method to deliver mRNA-encoded cargo to the nervous system directly through the nose,” Neely said.

Industry observers note that the mice appeared to tolerate the drops well, with no major side effects detected during the study. “Before we can trial this therapy in patients, we need to perform a series of safety studies in animals,” Neely stated. “It is a very promising pathway, but human noses are different from mouse noses, so we will need to test our drugs in humans to before we know whether it will work.

“We believe our new drug, if it works in humans, can promote general cognitive health as people age, should help treat a variety of neurodegenerative diseases, and may even increase cognitive abilities in healthy young people.”.

It has been revealed that the team plans to refine the delivery system and assess its long-term safety and effectiveness. “Based on previous clinical trials, we know the components used in this study to be safe in humans,” Neely stated. “We hope we can move rapidly through the requisite safety studies and trial this treatment in humans in the next two years.”.

According to recent reports, reference: “Bdnf mRNA-LNP Drives Nasal Epithelial BDNF Production and Improves Cognition in Aged and Alzheimer’s Disease Mouse Models” by Maria Bergamasco, Hannah Scarborough, Anna Ponta, Teleri Clark, Scott B. Cohen, Lipin Loo, Kazuma Fujikake, Rebecca Carr, R.M. Damian Holsinger and G.Gregory. Neely, 18 November 2026, Advanced Science. DOI: 10.1002/advs.78225.

Funding was received from the National Health and Medical Research Council, the NSW Ministry of Health and an ongoing philanthropic donation from Dr John and Anne Chong to support the work of the Neely Lab.

Disclosure: Greg Neely and Maria Bergamasco are inventors on a provisional patent application related to this work.

Tech Report: 2026 Was the Year Restaurants Went Full Midwest

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality.
  • Recent findings suggest that at Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve.
  • Sources indicate that the Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality.

Recent findings suggest that at Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve. Topped with glazed seasonal veggies, kernels of sweet corn in summer and sliced honeynut squash in late fall, it speaks to Knall’s Midwestern-meets-French approach—one of the reasons why his restaurant earned a slot on Eater’s 2026 list of the Best Latest Restaurants in America.

Sources indicate that the Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation. The Best Latest Restaurants list includes Chicago’s Creepies, which also digs into that Midwest-French mashup, and Kansas City’s Akoya Omakase, which brings a distinct viewpoint to the omakase experience. Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year, and Chicago’s Bad Butter, a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries. It even includes drinks—Culebra, a Puerto Rican spot that draws on the Latinx influences of its Chicago neighborhood, is on Punch’s Best New Bars list. Between these accolades and other national recognition, all eyes are on the Midwest right now. And that’s even before we get into the impact of the Chicago-set show The Bear, which put Italian beef on everyone’s radar, and the rise of tavern-style pizza around the country.

In a recent development, the Midwest has always had great restaurants, of course, but it’s undeniable that something has shifted. “People are flying into these cities rather than flying over them,” states Vinnie Cimino, the Cleveland chef who co-owns Rosy and Cordelia. “I think that word is getting out about these smaller pockets of culture and cuisine.” Some of this is attributable to diners being more willing to explore outside big coastal cities, but it’s also due to chefs returning home to the region. “Post-pandemic, a lot of folks moved out of larger cities and back home,” says Cimino. “Now they’re setting up shop and creating great things in the spaces that they grew up in.” David Posey, chef and co-owner of Creepies and Elske in Chicago, agrees, adding: “For a long time, it felt like we were playing catch-up with trends on the coasts. Now I think we’re less quick to follow trends and are more confident in having our own voice of what the Midwest is.”.

In a recent development, one of those chefs who left Upcoming York is Knall, a Birmingham, Alabama, native who cooked at Gramercy Tavern in New York before moving to his wife’s hometown of Milwaukee in 2020. Another is Peter Hoang, who worked at his father’s Kansas City, Missouri, sushi restaurant before gaining experience in Chicago and New York restaurants. When he returned to open Akoya Omakase, he crafted menus with the audience in mind, with two omakases, priced more affordably than many at $85 and $165, as well as an à la carte menu. “My sushi is honed by Japanese techniques and sourcing,” he indicates. “But I interpret what I think is best for the fish, whether that’s highlighting the textures and flavors through different garnishes or using aging or salting techniques.”.

It’s not simply that these are good restaurants located in the Midwest—these restaurants are deeply Midwestern in ethos. In Chicago, David and Anna Posey, who run the Michelin-starred Elske, wanted to open a French bistro for their second venture. But as they developed Creepies with chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski, David Posey claims they began expanding its focus: “We started taking flavors and adapting them to things that we’re a little more familiar with.” This means dishes that draw on the traditions of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Illinois—think tarte flambée on a tavern-style pizza crust and mussels with giardiniera. And it’s not just the food at Creepies that reflects the Midwest: “We told our designer that our inspiration board was a Midwest basement with wood paneling and low ceilings meets a bistro in the French countryside.”.

At Cordelia, Cimino leans into the traditional cuisine of Northeast Ohio, with offerings like raw-beef cannibal sandwiches and kielbasa with cabbage salad. “It’s the familiar flavors that we grew up eating, rethought into this more modern light,” he indicates. Meanwhile, Rosy “is a deeper dive into the culture of our region” and features dishes like Balkan cevapi and Italian cotechino cooked over live fire. The approach is drawing a wide range of Cleveland diners, from 20-somethings there for the cool, candlelit vibe to grandparents there to taste the food they grew up with. “I think that’s what the Midwest is,” Cimino says. “Being able to be that transgenerational space everybody feels welcome in.”.

It has been revealed that that welcoming community sensibility is a key component of Midwestern restaurants. Knall counts several farmers and shoppers at the West Allis Farmers Market, where he sources for Cassis, as some of his regulars. “To me, it demonstrates that’s really what Midwest food is: supporting those communities,” he says.

Perhaps more than anything, it’s hospitality that sets these spots apart. “Hospitality is our biggest focus between both restaurants and maybe even more of a focus than the food,” Knall claims. “To me, the way that our team makes you feel in the restaurants is such a Midwest thing.” And at Cordelia, where the slogan is “Midwest Nice,” Cimino says: “It’s welcoming you into our proverbial home.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • People who lived to 100 carried a distinctive chemical fingerprint in their guts, and boosting the bacterial enzyme linked to it helped older mice respond better to insulin.
  • Recent findings suggest that A single dose of engineered gut bacteria made older mice more sensitive to insulin about five months later.
  • The study focused on bile acids, which the liver makes to help digest fats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People who lived to 100 carried a distinctive chemical fingerprint in their guts, and boosting the bacterial enzyme linked to it helped older mice respond better to insulin.

Recent findings suggest that A single dose of engineered gut bacteria made older mice more sensitive to insulin about five months later. The UC San Diego team also analyzed data from young adults, older adults, and centenarians to see how the same gut bacterial activity varies with age in people.

The study focused on bile acids, which the liver makes to help digest fats. Bile acids also carry signals that help regulate metabolism, inflammation, and the body’s internal clock. Gut bacteria make enzymes called bile salt hydrolases (BSH) that change the chemical makeup of bile acids and can alter the signals they send.

Industry observers note that older mice indicated more microbial activity linked to BSH and more extensive changes to their bile acids than younger mice. The researchers then looked for a similar pattern in existing data from 48 young adults, 107 older adults, and 125 centenarians.

Industry observers note that centenarians had higher ratios of certain modified bile acids than either of the younger groups. Their gut microbiomes also contained more copies of a gene linked to BSH activity than those of older adults.

“Many studies of aging focus on what goes wrong as we get older, but our findings suggest that some changes in the gut microbiome may actually represent the body’s attempt to preserve metabolic health,” mentioned senior author Amir Zarrinpar, MD, PhD, Stuart and Barbara L. Brody Endowed Chair in Circadian Biology and Medicine and professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine. “If we can identify those beneficial functions and safely strengthen them, we may eventually be able to develop new ways to promote healthier aging.”.

Recent findings suggest that to test whether boosting BSH activity could change metabolism, the team gave 82-week-old mice a strain of gut bacteria engineered to keep making the enzyme. The bacteria took hold after one treatment and continued producing BSH over time.

Recent findings suggest that about 20 weeks later, the mice responded significantly better to insulin and were modestly better at clearing glucose from their blood than mice given a matched control bacterium. By week 32, the treated mice also indicated changes consistent with lower body weight, less body fat, and more lean mass.

Other measurements suggested that the mice used more fat for energy and that their mitochondria worked better. The researchers also saw shifts in the activity of genes involved in inflammation and the body’s internal clock.

Centenarians and aged mice represent different stages of life, and the mouse experiment did not establish whether the treatment extends lifespan. Studies in people will need to determine whether higher BSH activity helps preserve health with age, reflects healthier aging, or both.

Sources indicate that the researchers plan to test how different forms of the enzyme affect bile acid metabolism, inflammation, and energy use. They also want to see whether female mice respond similarly, given known differences in how males and females age.

Industry observers note that “The goal isn’t simply to live longer—it’s to understand the biology that allows some people to remain resilient as they age,” mentioned Zarrinpar. “The microbiome gives us an intriguing opportunity because, unlike many aspects of aging, it may be something we can modify. This study gives us a starting point for asking whether beneficial microbial functions can be amplified to help preserve metabolic health later in life.”.

Reference: “Microbial bile acid deconjugation counters metabolic decline in aging” by Ana Carolina Dantas Machado, Wuling Zhong, Anand R. Saran, Baylee J. Scientists Develop a Powerful Two-in-One Treatment for Gum Disease

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gum disease can eat away at the bone that holds teeth in place, and a tiny cage made of DNA helped slow that damage in rats.
  • Researchers at Sichuan University built a DNA carrier that delivers two compounds together to treat periodontitis, a chronic form of gum disease and a leading cause of tooth loss in adults.
  • According to recent reports, periodontitis starts when bacterial plaque builds up beneath the gums.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gum disease can eat away at the bone that holds teeth in place, and a tiny cage made of DNA helped slow that damage in rats.

Researchers at Sichuan University built a DNA carrier that delivers two compounds together to treat periodontitis, a chronic form of gum disease and a leading cause of tooth loss in adults. The team, led by Geru Zhang, Yunfeng Lin, and Xiaoxiao Cai, published its findings in the International Journal of Oral Science.

According to recent reports, periodontitis starts when bacterial plaque builds up beneath the gums. The resulting immune response can gradually destroy the tissue and bone that anchor teeth. Deep cleaning and antibiotics can reduce the number of bacteria, but they may leave existing damage unrepaired and do not always stop the disease from progressing.

“We aimed to create a multifunctional DNA nanoplatform capable of delivering both curcumin and the antimicrobial peptide defensin directly to periodontal tissues, with the goal of overcoming the limitations of existing therapies,” Zhang said.

The team loaded both compounds into tiny, four-sided DNA structures called tetrahedral framework nucleic acids (tFNAs). The researchers tested the resulting complex, called Cur-de-tFNA, against bacteria linked to periodontitis and used a bacterial molecule to trigger inflammation in human periodontal ligament stem cells (PDLSCs) in the lab.

“The DNA carrier enhanced the stability and cellular uptake of curcumin while protecting defensin from degradation, allowing both therapeutic agents to function more effectively,” Lin said.

Industry observers note that in lab tests, the combined treatment outperformed its individual components across several experiments. It acted against bacteria linked to gum disease, reduced oxidative stress, and dampened an inflammatory signaling pathway called TLR4/NF-κB. It also increased levels of proteins involved in bone formation.

In a recent development, in rats with periodontitis, the treatment reduced bone loss and inflammatory damage around the teeth. The researchers observed less activity from cells that break down bone, along with more collagen deposition and newly introduced bone formation. “As a result, the nanoplatform delivered stronger antimicrobial activity, better control of inflammation, and improved preservation of periodontal tissues in preclinical models,” Cai said.

In a recent development, the biodegradable DNA carrier was well tolerated in preclinical tests. Human trials are needed to determine whether the treatment is safe and can help preserve or rebuild the tissues that support teeth.

Reference: “DNA framework-based nanomedicine platform: a triple-function strategy for treating periodontitis via antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and osteogenesis-promoting activities” by Geru Zhang, Weitong Cui, Haoyan Wu, Xiaowei Liu, Liwei Huang, Yunfeng Lin and Xiaoxiao Cai, 29 April 2026, International Journal of Oral Science. DOI: 10.1038/s41368-026-00439-2.

This study was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the National Natural Science Fund for Young Scientists Fund Program C, the Postdoctoral Fellowship Program, the Sichuan Science and Technology Program, the Sichuan Province Youth Science and Technology Innovation Team, the Health Commission of the Sichuan Province Medical Science and Technology Program, the Sichuan Province Innovative Talent Funding Project for Postdoctoral Fellows, the Sichuan Provincial Natural Science Youth Foundation, and Sichuan University.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, indicates Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

Industry observers note that the answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin states. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Sources indicate that meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

Industry observers note that in separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin indicates.).

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin claims. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

Recent findings suggest that it’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.
