The 8 Best Solar Generators Provide Reliable Backup Power in a Pinch

📅 13 Aug 2021 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel.
  • Sources indicate that unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

Sources indicate that unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

According to recent reports, despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

To pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

In a recent development, our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also key—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

According to recent reports, very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

It also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it indicates 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

In a recent development, while 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

As a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review.

This model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The new version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

In a recent development, expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

Industry observers note that the newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

Sources indicate that the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

This power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

It also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

If there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review.

Recent findings suggest that the EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

According to recent reports, to get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

Like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

It has been revealed that we were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

Sources indicate that the Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

It has been revealed that one of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

Industry observers note that we got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

In a recent development, as a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review.

The latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

According to recent reports, there’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

Recent findings suggest that to test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

Of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings showed anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

Full Goal Zero Yeti 1500 Review.

In a recent development, the Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

In a recent development, another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

According to recent reports, for solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review.

In a recent development, power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

According to recent reports, meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

Recent findings suggest that for example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

Recent findings suggest that keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

Just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

It has been revealed that your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

Sources indicate that while weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

Sources indicate that that stated, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase quickly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you strategy to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

This is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

It has been revealed that A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

Sources indicate that I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

Solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

#170207. Breaking: Eagles Hunting Human-Sized Baboons Challenge Long-Held Evolutionary Theory

Breaking: Eagles Hunting Human-Sized Baboons Challenge Long-Held Evolutionary Theory

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Evidence of eagles hunting adult baboons suggests that aerial predators may have helped shape how early humans learned to communicate and protect one another.
  • In a recent development, in the middle of the Sahara, researchers have found evidence that eagles are killing primates as large as some of our early ancestors.
  • Eagles have hunted primates for millions of years, yet no primate weighing more than 13 kilograms (29 pounds) had previously been confirmed to have been killed by a bird of prey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evidence of eagles hunting adult baboons suggests that aerial predators may have helped shape how early humans learned to communicate and protect one another.

In a recent development, in the middle of the Sahara, researchers have found evidence that eagles are killing primates as large as some of our early ancestors. One of the apparent victims, an adult male baboon, was estimated to have weighed more than 26 kilograms (57 pounds), challenging a long-held assumption about the dangers early humans faced.

Eagles have hunted primates for millions of years, yet no primate weighing more than 13 kilograms (29 pounds) had previously been confirmed to have been killed by a bird of prey. Scientists believed that humans and their ancestors had escaped this threat for roughly the past 2.5 million years because they were too heavy for even the giant eagles of the past to lift.

Industry observers note that the discovery comes from the Ennedi Plateau in northern Chad, where an isolated population of baboons lives in the Sahara Desert. Researchers from the University of St Andrews traveled to the region with colleagues from Dartmouth College, the University of Konstanz, the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, and African Parks.

Sources indicate that lead author Professor Catherine Hobaiter, from the School of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of St Andrews, said, “This was such an extraordinary expedition, any primatologists dream! Some of the baboons there are so remote they rarely, if ever, see people, and so after a couple of days they ended up following us around—we were probably the most interesting thing they’d seen for a while!”.

Sources indicate that she added: “We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them. Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

In a latest study published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, the researchers describe finding the remains of adult male baboons with telltale signs of eagle predation, including talon punctures in their skulls and distinctive scrapes and rake marks on their shoulder bones.

Senior author Professor Nathaniel Dominy from Dartmouth College noted, “At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t. Our skepticism slowly gave way to acceptance. The evidence was convincing.”.

The behavior of the living baboons offered another clue.

Professor Hobaiter explained, “One of the most exciting observations was seeing the baboons respond when a pair of Verreaux’s eagles swept overhead—primates are very specific about only responding to eagles that are a genuine threat. We’d seen them very relaxed around other big birds of prey, but as soon as the Verreaux came into view they alarm called and dropped down to safety.”.

Recent findings suggest that for scientists studying human evolution, the possibility of attacks from above is particularly interesting. Primates defend themselves differently against eagles than they do against predators such as significant cats and crocodiles. One strategy, known as mobbing, involves primates, particularly larger adult males, charging an attacker to drive it away. If our ancestors faced similar threats, eagles may have helped shape the evolution of communication and group cooperation.

Many primates living in areas where eagles hunt also travel in large groups alongside other primate species. For much of our evolutionary history, our ancestors shared their surroundings with other early human species and primates. Although these relationships are often viewed in terms of competition, protection from predators may have given them a reason to stay together.

Dr. Gisela Kopp, from the University of Konstanz and the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, said, “Primatology often focuses on regions with a high diversity of primates, but shifting our attention to a place where no primatological data has ever been collected before, proved to be extremely rewarding.”.

In a recent development, dr. Jean Didier Akpona, from African Parks, said, “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence. This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”.

The researchers are eager to continue studying the isolated baboon population, whose unusual lifestyle is already challenging several assumptions about the species.

Professor Hobaiter added, “Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what new ‘rules’ they’ll break next!”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Signs of Eagle Predation on a 22-kg Adult Primate” by Catherine Hobaiter, Tewogbade J. D. Akpona, Gisela H. Kopp and Nathaniel J. Dominy, 18 November 2026, American Journal of Biological Anthropology. DOI: 10.1002/ajpa.70377.

The 7 Best Garage Heaters for Your Workshop

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, garages and unfinished basements are often poorly insulated, making them prone to extreme cold in fall and winter.
  • Garage heaters come in various styles, though the most popular models are electric and propane.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, garages and unfinished basements are often poorly insulated, making them prone to extreme cold in fall and winter. A garage heater can turn this typically frigid space into a warm, practical area for woodworking projects, vehicle maintenance, and more. If you strategy to spend time in your garage this winter tackling projects at your workbench, raising the ambient air temperature is a must.

Garage heaters come in various styles, though the most popular models are electric and propane. Electric heaters are convenient and easy to install if a power outlet is nearby. Propane heaters are more portable and can cover more surface area. Natural gas garage heaters are also powerful options for larger garages and can offer long-term heating solutions.

Heaters can benefit not only comfort but also safety. Cold temps can cause condensation to collect on tools and stored items, which may lead to rust and other damage. Wintry environments can also cause car engines and batteries to wear out faster. A well-heated garage protects your investments and provides a warmer, safer place to work.

If you're ready to prep for winter weather, read on for our in-depth reviews of the best garage heaters, followed by the most crucial things to know before buying.

Industry observers note that although we haven’t tested the models below ourselves, we applied our experience testing space heaters and patio heaters to supplement our search for the best garage heaters. We spent a lot of time vetting features and specs, checking manufacturer websites, gauging prices, and consulting user reviews before deciding which ones made the cut. We spoke with mechanical and electrical engineering experts to understand what makes a great garage heater, and we considered heat types (electric, propane, or kerosene), as well as whether the heaters are permanent or portable.

This 240-volt compact garage heater is the best all-around choice for most spaces, with 7,500 watts of heating power and the option to mount it on the wall or ceiling.

According to the manufacturer, it warms a typical garage or unheated building to between 50 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit and should be installed with a foot of clearance from combustible surfaces.

The garage heater’s adjustable louvers let you direct air where you need it most, and a remote-controlled thermostat is built into the front of the heater. A wall-mounted thermostat is available for the unit as well, but it’s sold separately.

Recent findings suggest that thanks to its Wi-Fi capability, you can operate this heater from virtually anywhere to ensure your garage is warm when you get home, or to heat the space before you spend time at your workbench. You can turn the unit on and off and set recurring schedules through the app.

The garage heater is rated to warm a 1,000-square-foot area, with an adjustable output of up to 20,000 BTUs. It can be mounted to the wall or ceiling, and its large digital temperature display is easy to read, even from across the room.

But for the price, it’s disappointing that the garage heater doesn’t include wiring.

For a powerful 5,600-watt portable garage heater, we recommend this NewAir model. It’s designed to warm spaces up to 600 square feet, and it includes a 6-foot cord that neatly coils on top of the unit, with brackets to hold it down.

Sources indicate that the fan has two settings: automatic (which turns on when the heating element activates) and continuous. You can switch between the two manually.

Use continuous mode to keep air moving in spaces with high ceilings or when you’re operating an air-cleaning appliance, like a bench-top air filter, as it helps push dusty air through to speed up the process.

In a recent development, designed for outdoor areas like patios, this Briza heater still works well in a garage thanks to its dust-resistant properties. It comes with an adjustable tripod that you can set between 44 and 84 inches tall. Selecting between its three heat settings—900, 1,200, or 1,500 watts—is easy with the unit’s remote control.

Sources indicate that the heater has a built-in safety sensor that automatically shuts the appliance off if it tips over. A timer provides additional safety (and energy savings) by automatically shutting the heater off after 1 to 9 hours of operation.

For a compact, affordable garage heater ideal for targeted heating, this propane-fueled unit from Mr. Heater is a great choice. It delivers 4,000 to 9,000 BTUs from a single 1-pound liquid propane canister and can heat up to 250 square feet. It works great on the floor by your workbench or desk.

The heater can run for up to three hours on high, or you can upgrade to a 20-pound tank with a separately sold adapter. The heater’s size and weight make it easy to reposition, and it’s easy to bring with you to a shed, campsite, or other workspace.

This heavy-duty, 240-volt garage heater is ideal for climates with major temperature swings, featuring a two-stage high-and-low heating system.

Its lower heat output suits mildly cool days, while the higher stage can warm garages in single-digit temperatures. It also has a fan mode ideal for increasing airflow in a potentially stuffy garage, plus an energy-saving setting that defaults to the lowest wattage to maintain the desired temperature.

A universal bracket is included for easy mounting to a ceiling or wall, and this heater has a remote-controlled thermostat. The only drawback is that it doesn’t offer much coverage for the price.

If you have an uninsulated wood garage or another minimally insulated space, this large, ceiling-mounted garage heater is worth a look.

In a recent development, it runs on natural gas (a propane conversion kit is included) and, with a built-in electric fan, can warm areas up to 2,000 square feet thanks to its impressive 80,000-BTU output. It also has a powered exhaust that allows for vertical or horizontal venting.

Note that the Substantial Maxx does not come ready to install; you’ll have to purchase a thermostat, gas hose, fittings, and regulator separately. For most people, it’s best to have a licensed heating-cooling contractor install this garage heater.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a lot to consider when using a heater to keep your garage safe and comfortable. So we picked the brain of Pat Porzio, a mechanical engineer and multi-licensed tradesman (electrical, plumbing, HVAC). He’s also the HVAC manager for Russo Brothers in East Hanover, New Jersey. We also spoke with David Shapiro, an electrician, author, and expert on old house wiring who contributes to electrical product and installation standards.

In a recent development, both agree on one thing: Your overarching concern in heating a garage is safety. The first words out of both their mouths were identical: “Pull a permit.” That is, if you strategy to use a permanently installed electric or gas-fired garage heater, you need to file a building permit for the work—whether you do the work yourself or hire a contractor. Permitted installations are inspected by the town or other authority with jurisdiction over this work where you live, which increases the likelihood of a safe installation.

According to recent reports, aside from pulling a building permit for the electrical work, Shapiro steers homeowners away from any heater without a UL (or other safety-related U.S. testing agency) listing.

It has been revealed that using a 120-volt space heater is simpler; same goes for small propane-fired and kerosene heaters. You don’t need a building permit to use one of these in a garage. Still, there are safe and unsafe ways to use these heaters. For more on that topic, check out our garage heater safety tips below.

Sources indicate that as we mentioned earlier, there are a couple of different types of garage heaters. Electric heaters are easier to install, don't require a vent, and are generally safer. But depending on your local electricity rates, they can be more expensive to run. Gas heaters use natural gas or propane, and they can be a more cost-effective option for heating larger garages. They require ventilation, which can be a pain if you don't already have the right setup.

Infrared heaters heat objects rather than the air, so they can be a good companion for localized projects at your workbench. Forced-air heaters use a fan to distribute heat quickly and work well for large spaces, but they require good insulation to run efficiently and may kick up dust around your workshop.

For most garages, an electric heater is often the most viable option because it's easy to install, safe, and effective. But if you have a larger or poorly insulated garage, a gas heater might be the way to go.

Industry observers note that “A bigger heater is not necessarily better,” Porzio states. “An oversized heater will short cycle. That is, it will turn on and off too frequently. It satisfies heating demand very promptly and abruptly turns off. A heater that is too small will do just the opposite. It will run and run and never fulfill the heating demand, eventually wearing itself out.”.

In a recent development, before contractors install a boiler or furnace, they perform a series of calculations, called a Manual J, to determine the correct size. While homeowners can get a rough estimate by multiplying the area's square footage by 50 to get the required BTUs, Porzio recommends using simplified Manual J forms online or a sizing tool like those on King-Electric.com and Newair.com.

For reference, a two-car garage will need a heater ranging from 30,000-50,000 BTUs to reach a consistent, comfortable temperature.

Industry observers note that whether you attempt the electrical work or hire it out, Shapiro has two more recommendations. First, don’t install the heater so that a power cord leading to a machine or tool could be draped directly in front of it. The heat can damage the cord.

Recent findings suggest that second, consider installing a CO alarm in the garage. A CO alarm can make the garage a safer place to work, especially if you’re heating it with gas, and it can also protect the occupants of the house.

Glaciers Are Melting at Alarmingly Different Rates and Climate Alone Can’t Explain Why

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Where a glacier ends can influence how rapidly it disappears, with implications for communities that depend on mountain meltwater or face the threat of flooding.
  • In a recent development, between 2000 and 2020, the number of lakes in direct contact with glaciers worldwide grew by about 35 percent.
  • In a recent development, an international research team, including Tobias Bolch from the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), used artificial intelligence to map glacial lakes from satellite images taken in 2000 and 2020.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Where a glacier ends can influence how rapidly it disappears, with implications for communities that depend on mountain meltwater or face the threat of flooding.

In a recent development, between 2000 and 2020, the number of lakes in direct contact with glaciers worldwide grew by about 35 percent. Their expansion has consequences for the ice that remains. Lake water can melt glaciers from underneath, while chunks of ice can break away and fall into the water. Until recently, scientists had struggled to determine how much these processes contribute to glacier loss worldwide.

In a recent development, an international research team, including Tobias Bolch from the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), used artificial intelligence to map glacial lakes from satellite images taken in 2000 and 2020. The researchers manually checked the results, distinguishing lakes that touched glaciers from those already separated from the ice. Their findings were published in Nature Climate Change.

Recent findings suggest that over the 20-year period, glaciers ending in lakes lost an average of 66 centimeters (26 inches) of water equivalent annually, meaning the lost ice would produce a layer of water that deep. By comparison, glaciers ending on land lost 40 centimeters (16 inches), and those ending in the sea lost 36 centimeters (14 inches).

Recent findings suggest that “Our research has shown that contact with a lake further accelerates the loss of ice from a glacier,” states Tobias Bolch. “While the climate and the topography of the glacier are the most significant factors influencing glacial mass loss, lakes significantly exacerbate it.”.

In a recent development, the number of lakes touching glaciers increased by more than 3,500, with particularly pronounced expansion in Alaska and the southern Andes. Their combined area grew by around 600 square kilometers (232 square miles). They also gained an estimated 66 cubic kilometers of water, enough to submerge the entire city of Vienna under approximately 160 meters (525 feet) of water.

In a recent development, using machine learning models, the researchers found that glacier characteristics such as elevation and slope accounted for 46 percent of the explained influence on ice gains and losses. Temperature, precipitation, and other climatic factors accounted for around 43 percent, while glacial lakes contributed approximately 11 percent.

“The findings from this study will help us to estimate future changes to the glaciers more accurately,” says Tobias Bolch. “This is particularly crucial for mountainous regions and their forelands, where meltwater is a significant source of water. Such findings are also relevant when assessing the risks posed by glacial lakes in the event of potential outbursts.”.

Industry observers note that reference: “Climate and glacier geometry dominate global glacier–lake interactions” by Shaochun Zhao, Guoqing Zhang, Matthias Huss, Georg Veh, Jonathan L. Carrivick, Tobias Bolch, David R. Rounce, Qian Tang, Yifan Bu, Yan Song, Menger Peng, Xue Wang, Xinhai Zeng, Danni Huang, Mengjie Zhu, Tao Zhou and Jie Cheng, 20 November 2026, Nature Climate Change. DOI: 10.1038/s41558-026-02808-5.

This work was supported by grants from the Basic Excellent Research Group for Tibetan Plateau Earth System, National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC ERGTPES project no. 42588201), the National Key Research and Development Project of China (2024YFF0809104), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant no. 42571153), the Second Tibetan Plateau Scientific Expedition and Research Program (STEP, 2024QZKK0301), the Department of Science and Technology of the Tibet Autonomous Region (XZ202502JD0025, XZ202403ZY0028) and the High-Level Talent Program of Xizang University (XZDXDR202501).

Crowded Proteins Can Change How Enzymes Work

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Laboratory research suggests that nearby proteins can reshape enzymes, offering clues to how the physical environment inside our cells may help regulate the chemistry of life.
  • In laboratory droplets designed to mimic conditions inside cells, enzymes worked faster as the liquid became more crowded with proteins, up to a point.
  • Many of the chemical reactions that keep cells alive occur in the cytoplasm, where proteins and other molecules can gather into compartments without an enclosing membrane.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Laboratory research suggests that nearby proteins can reshape enzymes, offering clues to how the physical environment inside our cells may help regulate the chemistry of life.

In laboratory droplets designed to mimic conditions inside cells, enzymes worked faster as the liquid became more crowded with proteins, up to a point. Active enzymes also helped nearby molecules move more freely through the liquid.

Many of the chemical reactions that keep cells alive occur in the cytoplasm, where proteins and other molecules can gather into compartments without an enclosing membrane. Researchers from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST), in collaboration with the Max Planck Institute for Dynamics and Self-Organization (MPI-DS) and RIKEN, studied how enzymes interact with these crowded environments.

In a recent development, “What’s fascinating is that we can connect interactions between individual atoms to the movement of molecules across an entire droplet. Events at the smallest scales can shape, and be shaped by, the physical behavior of a much larger system,” claims senior author Professor Paola Laurino, who leads the Protein Engineering and Evolution Unit at OIST.

According to recent reports, the OIST researchers prepared tiny droplets containing different concentrations of a protein called bovine serum albumin (BSA). In separate experiments, they introduced two enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), along with their substrates, the molecules upon which the enzymes act.

Enzyme activity increased as more BSA was added to the droplets. Only at very high protein concentrations did crowding begin to interfere with the reactions.

“This initial increase in enzymatic activity seemed counter-intuitive, as you’d typically expect any level of crowding to impair movement of the enzymes and substrates and increase the liquid’s viscosity, therefore slowing down the reaction from the start,” explains Laurino.

In a recent development, laurino and her team also used fluorescent tracers to examine how enzyme activity affected the movement of molecules within the droplets. Both BSA proteins and fluorescent nanoparticles moved more freely in the presence of active enzymes. Droplets containing modified, inactive enzymes were more viscous, and molecules moved more slowly through them.

“Similarly, we found that higher concentrations of the enzymes or their substrates in the droplets also increased mobility,” indicates Professor Ramin Golestanian, director of the Department of Living Matter Physics at MPI-DS.

The researchers used fluorescent markers to track the movement of nanoparticles in the droplet. Credit: Dindo et al., 2026, 10.1038/s41467-026-77666-y.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations conducted by researchers at RIKEN suggested that crowding helped accelerate reactions by changing the shape of the enzymes. The simulations highlighted that the active site, the region where substrates bind and react, was open under dilute conditions and closed as the concentration of surrounding proteins increased.

In a recent development, “When closed, the energy barrier required was much lower, allowing the reaction to happen more readily,” explains Laurino. “To detect such a change in these simulations by MD was really surprising to us.”.

According to recent reports, researchers at MPI-DS developed a theoretical model to explain the increased movement within the droplets. They proposed that enzyme activity creates differences in chemical concentrations throughout the liquid, generating tiny flows.

“These flows allow the molecules to move more freely and mix within the droplet, highlighting how enzyme activity can potentially lead to physical effects across larger scales,” claims Golestanian.

Laurino plans to investigate whether these interactions also occur in complexes where several enzymes operate in close proximity. Her team will also conduct experiments in living bacterial cells to determine whether the findings hold under more complex biological conditions.

Sources indicate that reference: “Enzymes can activate and mobilize dense biomolecular condensates across scales” by Mirco Dindo, Jakob Metson, Weitong Ren, Michalis Chatzittofi, Kiyoshi Yagi, Alessandro Bevilacqua, Erika Fukuhara, Yuji Sugita, Ramin Golestanian and Paola Laurino, 30 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77666-y.

Funding: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University, Japan Society for the Promotion of Science, Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Japan, RIKEN.

By Anna Mattson and Science News Staff.

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor.

In a recent development, major thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” claims senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a new appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”.

In a recent development, staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with new parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”.

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Manufacturer | $29.99.

Industry observers note that adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham states.

Saul Justin NewmanThe MIT Press | $29.95.

In a recent development, senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen claims. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”.

Susana CarmonaThe MIT Press | $27.95.

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, new mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she indicates. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Aaron MahnkeRunning Press | $30.00.

Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century New England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”.

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00.

Conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover states. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole new light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”.

Riley BlackSt. Martin’s Press | $29.00.

In a recent development, tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”.

Joshua D. MezrichThe MIT Press | $29.95.

And for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”.

Physicists Crack a 44-Year-Old Nuclear Fusion Mystery

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have found a way to predict the heating requirements of future fusion machines, offering valuable insight into one of the biggest challenges of harnessing the energy that powers the Sun.
  • Sources indicate that in 1982, scientists studying nuclear fusion discovered something unexpected.
  • Industry observers note that nuclear fusion releases energy when light atomic nuclei combine, the same process that powers the Sun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have found a way to predict the heating requirements of future fusion machines, offering valuable insight into one of the biggest challenges of harnessing the energy that powers the Sun.

Sources indicate that in 1982, scientists studying nuclear fusion discovered something unexpected. Once the heating power inside an experimental fusion machine reached a certain level, the fuel suddenly became much better at retaining heat. This discovery offered a way to overcome one of the biggest challenges in fusion research. More than four decades later, predicting how much power is needed to trigger this change remains a difficult problem.

Industry observers note that nuclear fusion releases energy when light atomic nuclei combine, the same process that powers the Sun. Recreating this process on Earth requires heating a gas to extreme temperatures, turning it into plasma, a state of matter made up of electrically charged particles.

Recent findings suggest that machines called tokamaks use powerful magnetic fields to confine this plasma inside a doughnut-shaped chamber. However, keeping the plasma in place does not necessarily keep it hot. Turbulent motion within the plasma can carry heat away, making it difficult to maintain the conditions needed for fusion.

It has been revealed that the phenomenon discovered in 1982 occurs when heating power crosses a critical threshold, causing turbulence near the outer edge of the plasma to drop sharply. Scientists call this the transition from low confinement (L-mode) to high confinement (H-mode), a state in which the plasma retains energy much more efficiently.

In a recent development, achieving H-mode is essential for future fusion reactors. The difficulty is that the amount of heating power required depends on several factors, including how densely packed the plasma particles are and the direction of the magnetic field. Existing theories have struggled to explain both effects together.

In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Brenno De Lucca, a doctoral assistant at EPFL’s Swiss Plasma Center (SPC), developed a theory that explains these effects within a single physical framework.

In a recent development, using computer simulations, the researchers recreated the behavior of plasma inside a tokamak as heating power increased. They identified the physical processes responsible for the transition, developed a mathematical model to describe them, and compared its predictions with experimental measurements from existing tokamaks.

Their results demonstrated that turbulence generates flows within the plasma that move at different speeds across its outer region. As neighboring layers move past one another at different speeds, they help disrupt the turbulent motion that created them in the first place. This reduces heat loss, allowing the plasma to retain more energy.

The researchers also found that the direction of the magnetic field, the movement of the plasma, and collisions between particles work together to make H-mode easier to reach in one magnetic field configuration than in the other.

In a recent development, plasma density presents another complication. Increasing the density can reduce the amount of heating power needed in one range and increase it in another. The researchers derived equations describing these changes and other operating conditions, explaining why there is a particular density at which the heating requirement is lowest.

It has been revealed that the model could help researchers determine whether future fusion machines will have sufficient heating power to achieve H-mode. For ITER, the world’s largest international fusion project, presently under construction in France, the researchers predicted a minimum requirement of 43 megawatts, comfortably below its planned heating capacity of 73 megawatts.

The outlook is tighter for SPARC, a compact tokamak that uses powerful magnetic fields and is being developed by the U.S. organization Commonwealth Fusion Systems. Its predicted minimum heating requirement is 26 megawatts, slightly above its planned capacity of 25 megawatts, leaving considerably less room for uncertainty.

According to recent reports, reference: “Theory for the Power Threshold of the L−H Transition in Tokamaks” by B. De Lucca, P. Ricci, B. Labit, D. Mancini, L. N. Stenger and Z. Tecchiolli, 13 November 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/rw25-wy15.

Funding: EUROfusion Consortium, European Union Euratom Research and Training Programme (Grant Agreement No. 101052200), Swiss State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation (SERI), Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF), and Swiss National Supercomputing Center (CSCS).

Sources indicate that the crackle of a fire on a cold winter night can add charm to any home. However, fireplaces aren’t particularly efficient heat sources, especially in chilly temperatures. And electric fireplaces, space heaters, and other supplementary heat sources can leave you in the dark (and out in the cold) during a power outage.

Instead, consider adding a wood stove—an appliance that provides a country aesthetic and serves as a primary or secondary heat source. Modern wood stoves can be safe, affordable, and efficient if you clean and maintain them regularly.

Recent findings suggest that more than 2 million of the roughly 12.5 million wood stoves in the U.S. are older, uncertified models that put out far more particulate pollution than newer ones, according to the EPA, and some states prohibit or restrict these wood-burning devices. All of the wood stoves recommended here are EPA-certified, and they still crank out enough BTUs to make your home or cabin cozy.

Recent findings suggest that before you buy, think carefully about where you’ll install your stove. You’ll need proper clearance from combustible materials in walls and floors, and the stove’s weight has to work for your house.

It has been revealed that it shares many features with our Best Overall pick, including a firebrick-lined firebox and a non-catalytic secondary burn that keeps emissions within EPA standards. In a recent development, wood stoves come in all shapes, sizes, and designs. Choose one that suits your space in terms of style and efficiency. Here’s how to decide what you need in a wood stove and what you don't.

There are two types of modern wood stoves: catalytic and non-catalytic. Both reduce air pollution by reburning exhaust to limit emissions, but catalytic stoves use a different process that is slightly more efficient at this second burn. Non-catalytic stoves are popular because they’re less expensive and slightly more efficient at producing heat.

Because the cost of a wood stove with a catalytic converter is at the moment prohibitive for the average homeowner, the wood stove models we’ve recommended below are all non-catalytic.

More Hot Stuff: Smokeless Fire Pits • Fire Pit Tables • Portable Fire Pits • Heated Blankets.

The size of your wood stove matters not just for the space it can heat, but also for safety. Before you install a wood stove, check your state requirements for clearance. Federal guidelines stipulate that the stove should be installed at least 3 feet from any combustibles in the wall, ceiling, or floors.

If you have children, also consider how much clearance you might need around the stove for a child safety gate and where you plan to stack and store firewood.

British Thermal Units (BTUs) might sound fancy, but it's just a measurement of how much heat is being generated. This differs from the heating area of a wood stove because it refers to the energy the stove produces in an hour. A rule of thumb: You need 20 BTUs for every foot of space you want to heat. Use this online BTU calculator to dial in exactly how many thermal units your home needs.

It has been revealed that decide whether you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source or for supplemental heat in the winter. In general, a small wood stove can heat about 500 square feet, while a medium wood stove warms up to 1,000 square feet. A large model will heat a room of 1,500 square feet or more.

Industry observers note that more isn’t always better. To keep costs in check and your wood stove efficient, consider if you really need to heat every space in your home or just the living areas your family frequents.

Modern wood stoves are lighter than ever, but many large models can still tip the scales at several hundred pounds. Depending on the stove's weight, you may not be able to install it in a mobile home or in certain structurally vulnerable spots in your house. Instead, look for a wood stove approved for mobile homes by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

If your goal is an outdoor wood stove portable enough for camping or backpacking, choose a lightweight model with components that collapse into a compact package.

Sources indicate that the size of the logs and the kind of wood you put into your wood stove is about more than convenience or cost. It can also affect burn time and efficiency, which is especially important if you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source.

It has been revealed that generally, most wood stoves fit logs about 16 inches long and 3 inches in diameter. As you can imagine, wood stoves designed for smaller logs may leave you rolling up your sleeves and grabbing the axe more often than you might like.

Since 2020, nearly all new wood stoves sold in the United States must be certified by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to meet its 2020 emissions standards, which limit fine particle pollution to 2.0 grams per hour (2.5 g/h when tested with cordwood). All of the wood stoves we’ve recommended below meet this standard, and you can look up any model in the EPA’s database of certified wood-burning heaters.

In a recent development, A wood stove’s effectiveness in converting wood into heat is expressed as a percentage of combustion efficiency. Efficiency matters because it directly translates into how much wood you’ll burn to keep your home warm. Most modern EPA-certified stoves fall between 70 and 80 percent efficiency, and every few points add up over a full heating season in fewer logs split, stacked, and hauled inside.

In a recent development, from insulating the chimney to adhering to proper stovepipe clearance, to wall shields and floor pads, there’s quite a bit to do when you install a wood stove, and much of it is mandated by building codes and state or federal laws. To protect your safety, it's critical that you don't miss a step, which is why I recommend leaving the installation of the wood stove to a professional.

Clean your wood stove (and chimney) thoroughly and often to avoid creosote buildup, a highly flammable byproduct of burning wood.

According to recent reports, while cleaning your chimney, tidying up your wood stove is pretty straightforward. When the stove is cool, lay down a cloth or newspaper, then empty the ashtray and any ashes from the firebox into an ash bucket. Then wait at least 24 to 48 hours before you dump the ash bucket so any slightly warm embers don’t catch fire.

Industry observers note that you can wipe down the interior with a soft, wet cloth and use a chimney brush to scrub out the stovepipe and loosen any residue. If the exterior has rust, you can use a wire brush or sandpaper to remove it.

In a recent development, yes, you can leave a wood stove unattended for a few hours or overnight, but with some caveats. You should tamp down or mostly close some vents to ensure the fire stays under control. Also, shut and lock the door, and clear any objects from around the stove.

Just be aware that if you strategy to leave the fire unattended and it goes out overnight, you’ll have to restart it, which is harder than simply feeding a live fire.

Most latest wood stoves you can buy in the U.S. will be EPA-certified, but you should still check the packaging to verify.

In a recent development, EPA certification means the wood stove has been independently tested to meet a particulate emissions limit of no more than 4.5 grams per hour. If you have an old model that is not EPA-certified, check whether your state has a program that provides tax deductions for replacing your wood stove.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, whether you’re spotting deer while on a hunt or identifying backyard birds, a trusty pair of 10x42 binoculars is a must-have for the outdoors. The 10x magnification isn’t too tight for closer quarters—think birdwatching—but gives you enough reach to spot animals 1,000 yards away, and it’s even sufficient for casual stargazing. The 42 mm objective lens (the one farther from your eyes) is wide enough to let in lots of light while keeping the field of vision natural.

Most people want a pair of binoculars that is decent, but not so exceptional that they have to spend thousands. I recommend the $150 to $300 range to get high-quality glass with coatings and enough performance that you won’t ever feel the need to upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that both the Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 ($300) and the Leupold BX-3 ($230) fall right in this entry-level sweet spot. We tested both for our Best Binoculars buying guide and selected the Leupold BX-3 10x42 as our favorite binocular overall, but the Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 performed very well, considering the price (often available for much less than retail, as it’s an older model than the Leupold, which debuted this year). As such, we compared the two head-to-head to identify meaningful differences. Here’s what we found.

Vortex Crossfire vs. Leupold BX-3.

Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 Binoculars.

I tested the Crossfire and BX-3 both handheld and tripod-mounted side-by-side in a range of conditions including sunset low-light environments, dense forest, long-distance expanses in the mountains, and several specialized setups designed to test things such as chromatic aberration, color fidelity, and image sharpness.

Truly objective stats about binocular performance can be hard to come by, so the somewhat arbitrary “tiers” of binoculars defined by price and place in a company’s lineup can serve as useful shorthand for how impressive the optical quality is.

In a recent development, leupold’s BX-3 Alpine HD 10x42 binos are on the lower “budget” end of the organization's numbered BX lineup that goes all the way up to the $3,999 BX-6 Range HD RangeFinder 10x42 binoculars. Still, I would argue that this tier of binocular at 10x42 offers you most of the performance of the high-end models. The higher you go in price, in my experience, the smaller the gains in clarity and performance.

Sources indicate that vortex has many different lines, each one representing small jumps in features and optical quality. The Vortex Crossfire HD 10x42 sits between its Triumph and Viper lines—the Triumph is our Best Budget and the Viper is Best for Hunting. The Crossfire HD 10x42 is entry-level in terms of price but is likely to be all the binoculars most people need, and still feels like a significant cost if binoculars are a nice-to-have item for you.

In terms of size and specs, the Leupold BX-3 10x42 is likely most comparable to the Vortex Viper HD 10x42, but at $749 MSRP doesn’t feel like an apples-to-apples comparison. The Viper HDs are great binoculars, especially for hunters who demand the dawn and dusk performance, but their price is more than double that of the BX-3 Alpine HD.

It has been revealed that note that both brands’ binos are usually available at retailers for much less than the MSRP on the official sites. At the time of this writing, the $230 Crossfire can be had in several places for $150 while the $299 BX-3 binos are consistently $199 at Scheel’s and Cabela’s, making the two models fairly close on real-world price.

According to recent reports, both brands market to the hunting community and it shows in these fairly similar designs. The roof prism design on both the BX-3 and Crossfire is near-standard in this type of binocular and it helps keep the size and weight down compared to bulkier designs used in the cheapest binos.

In a recent development, the Crossfire binos have a slightly flared look as you move from the eyepieces to the exit lenses while the Leupold are straighter, but the overall form factor is very similar. The Vortex Crossfire is slightly longer at 6 inches compared to the 5.7-inch Leupold BX-3.

Practically, these are both relatively compact, lightweight binos that will fit in most any aftermarket chest harness and won’t cause neck strain as quickly as bigger glass. The Crossfire is 0.4 ounces heavier than the BX—not really a meaningful difference in practice.

It has been revealed that both have hard plastic eyecups by default, which are more durable than the floppy rubber ones that often come on the cheapest binos. Leupold’s BX-3, however, comes with two other swappable eyecup options. During sunrise and sunset glassing, when low-angle sunlight constantly sneaks into your peripheral vision and nukes contrast, the alternate eyecups block the intrusions, making a legitimately noticeable difference.

It has been revealed that this is the most important aspect of binoculars and also the hardest to objectively compare. Testing binoculars in person is always a smart idea if possible, as a few minutes scanning store shelves under artificial light isn't a great real-world test.

According to recent reports, both models provide decent center-image sharpness, especially considering their low cost. Moving closer to the edge of the image, clarity degrades in any binocular. The Leupold BX-3 binos have a slightly larger center area of sharpness than the Crossfire, perhaps 80 percent versus 70 percent.

A small but noticeable difference that subtly adds to the comfort of using them and gives Leupold an edge. In real-world use spotting animals such as bighorn sheep at long distances, I didn’t even notice. Like many marginal improvements you get with better binos, the sharper image just adds subtly to the overall picture clarity. For hunters, it’s unlikely to be the difference between success and failure, but it may make long sessions a touch easier and more enjoyable.

According to recent reports, I expected much more noticeable color fringing with the Crossfire HD, but it wasn’t pronounced in either pair. This defect in imagery in binocular views and photography occurs when light gets distorted and unnatural colors appear, usually around the edges of objects such as dark hair on an animal appearing blue or purple.

Both the Crossfire and BX-3 have HD in the name, which most likely refers to the glass elements and coating that help reduce glare, fringing, and generally produce a sharper image. For the most part, I noticed few differences in object sharpness and color. Both binos produce refreshingly neutral, natural colors in a range of light conditions.

Recent findings suggest that glare was less pronounced in the Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD than the Vortex Crossfire HD. Neither was able to eliminate glare entirely in challenging conditions such as pointing roughly 20 degrees off from the sun near sunset. But the portion of the view obscured by glare was smaller in the BX-3. It was also less hazy and diffuse, which left the portion of the view not obscured by glare clearer. This is, again, not a massive difference but adds incrementally to a slightly better optical quality overall for the BX-3.

Dusk, dawn, and dark forests are an extreme that can expose cheaper binoculars. For hunters, the crepuscular hours are when animals are usually most active—and when they’re hardest to pick out through your optics. Birdwatchers and casual consumers will be less affected if a bino struggles to gather dwindling light, but performance in these conditions is a reasonable indicator of overall optical quality.

In a recent development, the Leupold BX-3 was noticeably better in the worst, last-minute-of-the-day conditions, but the differences were only pronounced at the extremes. The brighter image wasn’t noticeable until well into the “blue hour” that comes before sunrise and after sunset. This makes using brighter optics much easier for hunters desperately scanning dwindling light but might not sway more casual owners. The brightness of the two pairs was mostly indistinguishable in midday sun.

Industry observers note that these are fairly closely matched binoculars, though the Leupold was the better pair whenever there was an edge to be had. The most meaningful separators were low-light brightness and center-image sharpness.

In a recent development, I didn’t find this surprising as the Leupold BX-3 Alpine HD costs more, and the Vortex Crossfire HD is more of an entry-level option that sits maybe one level below the BX-3 in the loose optical hierarchy of grades of binoculars. Rather than an apples-to-oranges comparison, testing these side-by-side served as a reminder of how subtle the improvements are between tiers and price jumps in the binocular world.

In a recent development, while dedicated hunters and birders might be willing to pay $50 to $100 more for the jump in quality to the BX-3, the affordability of the Crossfire HD will appeal to those who don’t need 10 percent better. Either pair presents a good value in their respective categories, but you’ll have to decide which you value more—a lower price or better performance in challenging conditions.
