Astronauts could turn everyday trash and moon dust into something surprisingly useful

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have combined paper fibers and simulated lunar dust to develop lightweight insulation that could be manufactured on the moon.
  • Trash on the International Space Station is bagged by astronauts and loaded onto a cargo ship.
  • The ship then either returns it to Earth or burns up in the atmosphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have combined paper fibers and simulated lunar dust to develop lightweight insulation that could be manufactured on the moon.

Trash on the International Space Station is bagged by astronauts and loaded onto a cargo ship.

The ship then either returns it to Earth or burns up in the atmosphere. On the moon, part of that waste might be put to use as insulation.

Paper fibers have now been ground together with imitation moon dust by a team of chemists.

The mixture was dried into an aerogel, an ultralight solid made mostly of empty space. Very little heat passes through such a material.

Recent findings suggest that according to the results, some insulation for a lunar base could be made on site. Two ingredients would be needed, and both should be plentiful there: waste paper and the ground outside.

In a recent development, the recipe was developed by Alexander Wei, a chemistry professor at Purdue University, and graduate researcher Jacob Staker. Their colleagues included researchers at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.

Wei mentioned a lunar settlement will generate waste rich in cellulose, the plant fiber found in paper and cardboard packaging.

“And I can guarantee that astronauts on the moon will never run out of moon dust,” Wei added.

For now, the aerogels exist only as samples made on Earth. A manufactured stand-in was used for lunar soil, and the paper was clean laboratory filter paper.

The final drying step relied on a method the team considers less practical on the moon than freeze-drying.

In a recent development, between 60% and 70% of wastepaper by weight is cellulose. When cellulose is torn into much finer threads, it can strengthen a material in ways the original fibers cannot.

It has been revealed that A stand-in for lunar soil, or regolith, has already been mixed with recycled plastic by other engineers. Wei’s team paired the dust with paper instead and used it as a grinding aid.

In a recent development, filter paper was first shredded in a food blender. The team then loaded it into a mill together with water, ceramic cylinders, and a powder called Lunar Highlands Simulant.

This powder is made from Earth rock to match soil from the moon’s highlands.

For two hours, the jars were spun at an acceleration about 60 times that of Earth’s gravity.

The team expects a mill of this kind to work in the moon’s weak gravity.

Industry observers note that the paper fibers were thinned by the ceramic cylinders alone. Once dust was added, they became much thinner still.

The most common fiber width fell to about 4 millionths of an inch (0.1 micrometers).

According to recent reports, fibers milled with dust were eight times thinner than those milled without it. They were also at least 30 times thinner than the original paper fibers.

The milled mixture was frozen in small molds, and its water was replaced with alcohol.

The team then removed the alcohol with pressurized carbon dioxide, which is a standard way of drying aerogels.

“Imagine an aerogel as a high-tech thermos for a lunar base,” Staker said. “Most of it consists of empty space that insulates the interior, helping it maintain the temperature of what’s inside.”.

Empty space accounted for 79.3% to 98.6% of the volume in these samples.

It has been revealed that in total, 18 batches were made, and the recipe was varied between them. Cellulose made up 1% to 9% of the wet mixture by weight. Dust made up 25% to 75% of the finished aerogel.

Insulation is rated by its thermal conductivity, which describes how easily heat passes through a material. A lower value is better.

The batches scored between 30 and 45 milliwatts per meter-kelvin when measured in air.

According to recent reports, an earlier attempt had produced a freeze-dried aerogel of imitation regolith and natural polymers. Its lowest reported figure was 70 in the same units.

The best fresh batches therefore had less than half the thermal conductivity of the earlier material.

The best insulation came from the batches with the least cellulose. Among the 18, the lightest batch was made from a mixture with 1% cellulose. Its conductivity of 30.9 was the lowest in that group.

When exposed to the moon’s near-vacuum environment, the pores would contain virtually no gas.

The team expects the aerogels to insulate better under those conditions. Several times less heat is conducted by other aerospace aerogels in a near-vacuum than in air.

Temperatures on the lunar surface can reach 266°F (130°C). That heat is a problem for many of the organic materials used in aerogels.

A sample heated in nitrogen did not start to break down until about 653°F (345°C).

Insulation and stiffness responded to the recipe in opposite ways. Heat was generally blocked best by the low-cellulose batches.

However, those batches were also soft, and they shrank the most during drying.

It has been revealed that A batch made with 1% cellulose came out 52% narrower than its mold. Only 3.2% shrinkage was seen in a batch made with 9% cellulose.

In a recent development, the stiffest batch was also made with 9% cellulose. Under compression, it was nearly 300 times stiffer than the softest batch.

“Rather than trying to make the world’s best aerogel, we’re looking for the sweet spot where we can get the properties we need with the limited resources we have available,” Wei said.

To look for that balance, the team fitted a statistical model to the 18 batches. Three recipes suggested by the model were then made and tested.

Dust would be far more plentiful on the moon than waste paper. For that reason, one recipe was required to be at least 60% dust by weight.

A figure of 61.2% was suggested by the model. The resulting aerogel had a conductivity of 30.5, which was the lowest in the study.

The same aerogel shrank by about half. It also did not meet the standards for the strength test.

Sources indicate that A second recipe was balanced across six measured properties. It insulated nearly as well, at 30.8, and shrank by 18.5%. This aerogel was stiff enough to be tested, but only 25% of it was dust.

The aerogels have not yet been made the way a lunar crew would make them. The team wrote that freeze-drying would be far more practical on the moon than the carbon dioxide method.

According to Wei, the lunar surface offers a natural vacuum and subfreezing temperatures at night. Wei remarked the water removed from the aerogel could also be recovered and reused.

In a recent development, however, this kind of material can be damaged by freezing. Growing ice crystals pack the fibers and dust together.

That packing is known to lower the quality of cellulose aerogels. To slow the growth of the crystals, the team proposed adding simple alcohols or sugars.

Recent findings suggest that only one kind of imitation dust was used, and the paper was not real trash. Every heat-flow measurement was taken at 73°F (23°C) in air.

For the weakest recipes, additives known to strengthen cellulose aerogels should be tested, the team suggested.

Sources indicate that freeze-drying is now being studied by the team for its next batches. Those tests should show whether a freeze-dried aerogel can insulate as well as the samples made so far.

The full study was published in the journal ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering.

Flying squirrels have an unusual habit that may shape entire forests

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Flying squirrels in China may influence where young trees grow by storing nuts in branches instead of underground.
  • Squirrels help oak forests grow by burying acorns and forgetting about them.
  • Instead of burying nuts, they tuck them between small branches.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flying squirrels in China may influence where young trees grow by storing nuts in branches instead of underground.

Squirrels help oak forests grow by burying acorns and forgetting about them. But two species of flying squirrel in southern China have a different way of storing food.

Instead of burying nuts, they tuck them between small branches. A new study suggests that this habit may affect where young trees grow.

Industry observers note that researchers found fewer seedlings a short distance from parent trees. But their numbers increased again about 66 feet (20 meters) away, where squirrels often store their nuts.

Sources indicate that scientists have usually linked this pattern to tree diseases. The new study suggests that squirrels may also play a role.

The work was carried out by Xuelian Tan, Han Xu and their colleagues at the Research Institute of Tropical Forestry. This institute is part of the Chinese Academy of Forestry in Guangzhou.

The study was a field survey of two tree species in a single forest. It therefore demonstrates a match between stored nuts and seedlings rather than proof that the squirrels planted them.

The research took place in Jianfengling, a forest within the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park on Hainan Island.

In a recent development, the forest averages about 67°F (19.7°C), and about 97 inches (2,461 millimeters) of rain falls there each year. In total, 992 species of free-standing trees and shrubs have been recorded in the forest.

Recent findings suggest that two of these trees are Cyclobalanopsis edithiae and Cyclobalanopsis patelliformis, which are close relatives of oaks. Their nuts are smooth and are not covered by the small cup at their base.

Many animals feed on these nuts. Their slick surfaces make them difficult to hold in place on a branch, however.

The flying squirrels solve this problem by gnawing grooves into the nuts, allowing them to wedge their food between branches.

The grooves differ between the two kinds of nut. Oval C. edithiae nuts usually receive one zigzag groove around the middle. Flatter C. patelliformis nuts, on the other hand, may carry up to 20 grooves on the underside.

Sources indicate that most stored nuts sat 33 to 82 feet (10 to 25 meters) from the nearest possible parent tree. Photographs in the latest study show squirrels returning to collect their nuts.

Another image reveals a gnawed nut that had fallen to the forest floor and begun to sprout.

Recent findings suggest that the importance of this behavior is linked to an older idea about how tropical forests work. During the early 1970s, the ecologists Daniel Janzen and Joseph Connell observed a pattern among tree seedlings.

Sources indicate that young trees, they noticed, were seldom found close to adults of their own species. The pair put this down to disease and pests.

Fungi and plant-eating insects that target one tree species spread from an adult tree to the seedlings around it.

Seedlings close to the parent are therefore more likely to die. Most seeds, however, land near the parent tree in the first place.

When both effects are combined, most surviving seedlings would be expected at a middle distance from the parent.

Recent findings suggest that ecologists refer to this process as conspecific negative density dependence. In simpler terms, plants tend to do poorly when they are surrounded by their own species.

This effect helps prevent any single species from dominating a forest. It is one reason why a rainforest can support so many different kinds of trees.

An earlier study in one of the Jianfengling plots detected the effect in 89% of tree species.

Where a seedling ends up hinges on two separate events. A seed has to land somewhere, and the young plant has to survive in that spot.

Seed-carrying animals can shift the first of these. Whether they could mimic the disease pattern on their own had gone largely untested.

Sources indicate that twenty parent trees anchored the survey. On ten of them, squirrels had lodged nuts in at least one direction.

The other ten were bare on all four sides. Each of the first ten trees got two survey lines.

Sources indicate that one pointed toward the stashed nuts, and the second ran off where no nuts hung. A single line from each bare tree, comparable in trunk size, formed a second point of comparison.

According to recent reports, markers went down every 16 feet (5 meters), stopping at roughly 100 feet (30 meters). Beside each marker lay three plots about a yard (1 meter) square. Every seedling inside those plots was tallied.

Recent findings suggest that seedlings along the test lines were most plentiful beside the parent tree. Their numbers, however, fell away at 16 and 33 feet (5 and 10 meters).

At 49 and 66 feet (15 and 20 meters), on the other hand, the counts climbed once more. Farther out they declined again, and the comparison lines showed no second rise at all.

Industry observers note that the 66-foot mark stood out in particular. There, the test lines held more seedlings than both comparison groups. The difference was statistically significant.

This is, notably, the very band of distances in which the squirrels hang their nuts. Beside the trunk itself, the test lines also held more seedlings, though only relative to the second group.

In a recent development, the authors offered a simple explanation, namely that trees ignored by squirrels may produce fewer nuts. Fewer nuts would mean fewer seedlings and, in turn, fewer squirrel visits.

Comparisons on two sides of the same tree therefore mattered, since seedling numbers vary widely from tree to tree.

Sources indicate that disease, for its part, ought to leave more damage on saplings close to the parent. Fine roots from 33 young trees were therefore examined, 15 of one species and 18 of the other.

The trees grew at different distances from adults. Each sapling’s root samples were inspected at 100 points under a microscope for lesions, which can indicate infection.

The level of damage, however, showed no clear trend with distance.

It has been revealed that fungi are not cleared by this result. Root lesions, the authors wrote, may not reflect the full pressure that pathogens place on seedlings.

They also wrote that “our results do not imply that pathogens are unimportant.”.

Squirrels that move nuts are, in their account, one more possible influence on where seedlings take root.

In a recent development, tan and Xu’s team has not confirmed whether squirrels directly help newly introduced trees grow. Other animals and local growing conditions may also play a role.

Changing how squirrels store nuts could provide stronger evidence, but such experiments are difficult in the wild.

The researchers suggest tracking seedlings over several years to see whether the nuts grow into healthy trees. Future studies could also examine other animals and forests.

The full study was published in the journal Forest Ecosystems.

Industry News: Standard fertility tests may be missing an vital clue about sperm health

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Retained mitochondrial DNA in mature sperm has been linked to longer times to pregnancy, even among men with normal semen test results.
  • In a recent development, men in couples who struggle to conceive are usually sent for a semen analysis.
  • A study of 327 men with normal semen results has now pointed to one extra factor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Retained mitochondrial DNA in mature sperm has been linked to longer times to pregnancy, even among men with normal semen test results.

In a recent development, men in couples who struggle to conceive are usually sent for a semen analysis. The test measures sperm count, concentration, shape and movement. Normal results do not guarantee a quick pregnancy.

A study of 327 men with normal semen results has now pointed to one extra factor. Some of their mature sperm still carried mitochondrial DNA.

According to recent reports, this DNA belongs to the mitochondria, the parts of a cell that make energy. Couples needed more time to conceive when the man’s sperm held more of it.

It has been revealed that the study was carried out at the Wayne State University School of Medicine in Detroit. It was observational, so a link was found but a cause was not established.

Sources indicate that the senior author was J. Richard Pilsner, a professor at Wayne State’s C.S. Mott Center for Human Growth and Development.

“These findings provide an important fresh window into the male contribution to reproductive success,” Pilsner mentioned.

It has been revealed that almost every cell in the body contains mitochondria. Energy for the cell is generated within these small compartments.

Mitochondria contain their own circular DNA, which carries 37 genes. In humans, it is passed on through the mother.

R. E. Giles and colleagues reported this maternal pattern in PNAS in 1980. Defects in these genes underlie several inherited diseases, and mitochondrial donation has been used to prevent their transmission.

According to recent reports, mitochondria are retained by the egg. According to a separate study, women’s egg cells keep this DNA largely free of age-related damage.

Recent findings suggest that in sperm, a different process is assumed. Most paternal mitochondrial DNA is thought to be eliminated during sperm production.

Industry observers note that that assumption sat awkwardly beside earlier data. Higher sperm mitochondrial DNA had been associated with lower semen quality and with longer times to pregnancy.

Recent findings suggest that two sources were proposed for the excess DNA. Ordinary body cells may have contaminated the samples, or immature sperm cells may have been present.

Purified, frozen sperm from the LIFE Study were analyzed by the Wayne State team. Couples in that cohort had been enrolled before conception and followed while they attempted pregnancy.

In a recent development, female partners kept daily journals. Time to pregnancy was then calculated in menstrual cycles.

Inclusion was restricted to men who met the 2010 WHO criteria for sperm count, concentration and shape. Of these, 327 were analyzed.

Mitochondrial DNA was quantified by digital PCR, a method that detects and counts individual copies of a target sequence.

Values ranged from 0.5 copies at the lower end to 49.0 copies at the upper end.

Recent findings suggest that bulk measurements cannot indicate which cells contain the DNA. Imaging of individual sperm was therefore required.

Samples from 18 men were selected at random, six from each of the low, moderate and high groups. Fluorescence in situ hybridization, which labels a chosen DNA sequence with a glowing tag, was adapted for sperm.

Recent findings suggest that image scoring was performed blind to group. A total of 50 sperm per participant were assessed.

It has been revealed that signal was located in the midpiece, a segment between the head and the tail. Mitochondria are arranged in a sheath around this segment.

Distinct spots were resolved around the midpiece in three-dimensional microscope images. Signal was not localized to the head or tail.

Jeffrey Mann, the study’s first author, is a postdoctoral fellow at Wayne State. He described the meaning of the images.

“Directly visualizing mitochondrial DNA within the sperm midpiece provides compelling evidence that the mitochondrial DNA detected by polymerase chain reaction reflects DNA retained within mature sperm,” Mann remarked.

Sources indicate that men with higher DNA levels had a larger share of glowing sperm. The correlation between the two measures was 0.87, where 1 would be a perfect match.

In men with moderate or high mitochondrial DNA levels, the glowing signals covered a larger area of the sperm midpiece than in men with low levels.

Sperm within a single sample differed from one another. In high-group samples, glowing sperm were found beside sperm with no signal.

A high reading appears to reflect a mixed population. Some sperm kept their mitochondrial DNA, while others removed it as expected.

DNA levels were then compared with the time each couple took to conceive. Higher levels were linked to a lower chance of pregnancy per menstrual cycle.

The team reported a fecundability odds ratio of 0.79. Values below 1 indicate lower odds of pregnancy per cycle as levels rise.

According to recent reports, differences between the low, moderate and high groups were unlikely to be due to chance. The link remained after adjustment for both partners’ age, body mass index and smoking.

Pilsner linked the imaging and pregnancy results.

“For the first time, we directly visualized mitochondrial DNA retained within mature sperm and showed that this feature is associated with lower likelihood of achieving pregnancy, even among men with normal semen parameters,” Pilsner said.

The team views the measure as a possible addition to routine semen analysis. A separate study found that body fat can lower sperm counts in men of normal weight.

“These findings suggest that conventional semen analysis may miss molecular signatures within sperm that provide important information about couples’ ability to conceive,” Pilsner said.

In a recent development, the study did not prove that retained DNA slows pregnancy. Only an association was shown.

Men with abnormal semen results were excluded. This limited the influence of other sperm problems on the findings.

The results cannot yet be extended to men with abnormal semen or diagnosed infertility.

Some factors were not measured. These included how often couples had sex, which also affects time to pregnancy.

Recent findings suggest that the probe detects specific DNA sequences. Whether each spot represents a complete mitochondrial genome or a fragment is still unknown.

Imaging was performed on only 18 men. The microscope images have been posted online for other researchers.

Future studies could test a link with TFAM, a protein that packages mitochondrial DNA. Retention in men with abnormal semen results could also be examined.

“This finding opens new questions about the molecular mechanisms that allow some sperm to retain mitochondrial DNA,” Mann remarked.

Normal semen results may not give a complete picture of male fertility. Leftover mitochondrial DNA in sperm could be worth measuring alongside the standard tests.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#170151. The prickly pear cactus has a surprising trick for surviving in the desert

The prickly pear cactus has a surprising trick for surviving in the desert

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1323 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered that tiny, short-lived leaves help prickly pear cacti capture carbon during the day and accelerate growth.
  • Cacti are usually described as plants that replaced their leaves with spines and thick green stems.
  • When rain finally reaches the desert, though, the prickly pear sprouts small green leaves on each new pad.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered that tiny, short-lived leaves help prickly pear cacti capture carbon during the day and accelerate growth.

Cacti are usually described as plants that replaced their leaves with spines and thick green stems.

When rain finally reaches the desert, though, the prickly pear sprouts small green leaves on each new pad. Within a few weeks, these are shed again.

According to recent reports, A team in Israel found that these leaflets behave like the leaves of a common garden plant. Carbon dioxide is taken in by them during the day.

The researchers estimate that they supply about a fifth of the carbon a young pad needs for growth.

So the cactus has two ways of gathering carbon rather than one. Older pads collect it after sunset, and the leaflets add to the supply once the sun is up.

The research was conducted by scientists at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) in Israel. They worked with researchers from the Gilat Research Center of the Volcani Institute.

Potted plants of Opuntia ficus-indica were grown for the experiments. This is the prickly pear species that is cultivated on farms.

In a recent development, the plants were kept in a net house on BGU’s desert campus at Sde Boker. They were watered every day for a year.

Ilya Gelfand is a professor at BGU’s Jacob Blaustein Institutes for Desert Research and a co-author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that “The cactus effectively has two gears,” said Gelfand. “Most of the year it runs in saving mode and breathes at night to hold on to every drop.”.

“When water arrives, it switches on a second, faster gear: temporary leaves that work by day like a regular plant. When the good times end, it simply drops them.”.

In most plants the tiny pores on the leaves are opened during the day.

In a recent development, carbon dioxide enters through them and is used by the plant to build sugars. Water is lost through the same openings, and that loss becomes costly in hot desert conditions.

Industry observers note that cacti, agave and many other succulents get by on less water because their pores open at night instead. The carbon dioxide is stored as an acid until the following morning.

The pores then close, and carbon dioxide released from the stored acid is used to make sugars with the help of sunlight.

Sources indicate that this strategy is known as crassulacean acid metabolism or CAM. Mature prickly pear pads rely on it so heavily that scientists classify the species as a full-time CAM plant.

The prickly pear is also an crucial crop that is grown on about 6.4 million acres (2.6 million hectares) worldwide.

It has been revealed that much of this area lies in drought-prone parts of Africa and South America. In these regions the plant is used for food and livestock feed and for slowing desertification.

According to recent reports, until this project, nobody had examined the leaflets as working organs. Each one measures only about 0.4 inch (10 millimeters) in length.

Around 150 of them can be carried by a single fresh pad, and they fall off after about six weeks.

The study was led by Patrick Mdemba, who is a doctoral student at BGU. Pores were the first thing he and his colleagues examined.

Clear nail polish was brushed onto pads and leaflets at five different times of the day. After the polish had dried it was peeled away and examined under a microscope. Each thin film preserved an impression of the pore openings.

The older pads opened their pores at night, which was the expected result for a CAM plant. The leaflets revealed the opposite pattern. Their pores were opened in the morning and closed after dark, as in a typical leafy plant.

According to recent reports, young pads that were two weeks old did not follow either pattern. Their pores were found to be open at every time the team checked.

Acid build-up between dusk and dawn was then measured in each tissue. A large amount was stored overnight in the older pads.

It has been revealed that the young pads stored more acid as they grew older. In the leaflets no significant difference was seen between the dawn and dusk readings.

Industry observers note that mdemba’s team also looked at the carbon inside the leaflets. Carbon in nature comes in a lighter form and a heavier form. Cactus pads that feed at night build up more of the heavier one.

In a recent development, in week-old leaflets the carbon looked much like the carbon in the pads. The mother pad had probably supplied it. Five weeks later the leaflets held noticeably more of the lighter form that daytime leaves collect.

For a second test the researchers sealed whole plants in a clear box almost 4 feet wide. They filled it with carbon dioxide made from the heavier form. One run lasted from 10 a.m. until noon, after the pads had closed their pores.

The marked carbon was found in the leaflets. The pads on those same plants gained no significant amount.

In a recent development, next came leaflets with no pad at all. Mdemba cut them from pads less than a week old and kept them in sealed jars on a sugar-free gel.

It has been revealed that in sunlight the carbon dioxide in each jar went down. Under aluminum foil it went back up. The cut leaflets also grew heavier until about day 15.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch as the leaflets.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch.

The team then worked out a carbon budget. A pad with about 150 leaflets gets roughly 0.12 grams of carbon a day from them. A 1998 study put a growing pad’s daily need near 0.6 grams. So the leaflets supply about 20% of it.

The leaflets covered their own growth first. What was left over went to the young pad.

Sources indicate that mdemba then took the leaflets away. All of them were cut off some young pads. On other pads they were left on but painted with clear nail polish, which sealed their pores.

In a recent development, pad size was checked every five days. By day 25 both groups were about a third smaller in area than normal pads. Pads with no leaflets also weighed about 38% less at three weeks.

Without working leaflets, then, a fresh pad grew more slowly.

“That lets the cactus grow quickly whenever the desert briefly allows it, without giving up its ability to survive drought,” said Gelfand.

Desert rain tends to arrive in short bursts. For desert plants the timing of that water can matter a great deal.

Some desert shrubs drop their leaves when life gets hard. The prickly pear makes its leaflets in the wet weeks and drops them within about two months.

Every plant in the study got water daily. That may have made the leaflets look more important than they would be in a dry field. Well-watered pads may rely less on their night feeding.

It has been revealed that the authors listed other limits too. They did not measure the two enzymes that capture carbon in each system. Gas exchange was not followed over a full 24 hours. Their conclusions come from pores, acid and carbon tracers instead.

They recommend measuring those enzymes in leaflets and young pads, along with gas readings around the clock.

According to recent reports, plants under drought stress should be tested as well. That work could show how much the leaflets matter when a wet spell is short.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Botany.
